en: The *Bṛhatī*,
composed by Prabhākara Miśra.
The second quarter of the first chapter.

The authority of the Veda has been stated with respect to that which establishes an object as something to be accomplished (*kārya*). But how can there be authority for that which expresses an object where no connection is perceived as being something to be accomplished—such as the passage "He wept" (*so ’rodīt*) and so forth? Let it not have authority; yet, its lack of authority does not [invalidate] the authority [of the rest of the Veda].

[The cognition] becomes invalid. For it has been stated that validity consists in independence; and the invalidity of another [cognition] does not cause that [independence] to depart from the valid one. Now, if you think that the validity of the entire Veda would not be established, [we reply:]...
By whom has this been asserted? The assertion is that whatever causes the comprehension of an object possesses the very definition of that [valid means of knowledge].
And that [definition] has been established through independence. However, where there is no comprehension of the object at all, that is simply not a valid means of knowledge. Because:

Or rather, it has been stated that for him as well, comprehension has as its object only that which is already cognized by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and thus its validity derives from that very source;
whereas in the case of the opposite, there is invalidity. Therefore, this inquiry—concerning how those [Vedic passages] whose purpose is not action [could have authority]—is entirely irrelevant.

If it is argued that because of the opposite of that [i.e., the lack of meaning], the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*) would be purposeless, we say no; for what is enjoined by the word *svādhyāya* is the act of studying, whether it be meaningful or meaningless— just as in the case of utterances such as *hum* and so forth.

Therefore, what is this objection? If it is argued that the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*) would result in being devoid of a purpose, that is not so; for what other purpose could there be for all injunctions than the fulfillment of the mandate (*niyoga*), and that is accomplished simply by the grasping of the syllables.
[The injunction] has been fulfilled. Furthermore, the knowledge of the meaning arises from the [text] itself, not because it is understood through the force of an injunction.

For there is no injunction for one who desires the knowledge of the meaning; nor is there, as in the case of cattle and such, any other established means of knowing the meaning of the Veda by which study would be enjoined for one desiring that [knowledge]. But is it not the case that, just like the Veda, the meaning of the Veda is also [known] from something other than one's own recitation (*svādhyāya*)?
Therefore, there is no established proof. For it is impossible to assert the causality of that which is unestablished.

If it were established, then all the more so, the prescription of such a desire would not be tenable; for it is precisely as an object of knowledge (*jñeya*) that it is desired, and [this applies to] what has already been known.

Desirability as an object of knowledge is not tenable. If it is argued that the injunction is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), we say no, because there is no lack of thorough knowledge from other sources. If it is argued that the word *svādhyāya* itself denotes the completion with the act of learning (*grahaṇāntataiva*), then who has said that the word *svādhyāya* denotes completion with learning? For in that case, there would be knowledge of the meaning even from what has not been learned.

There is no cognition of meaning from what has not been apprehended, because in the absence of apprehension there is only the apprehension of the phonemes (*varṇa*). If it is argued that this is due to the comprehension of the sentence (*vākya*), then the sentence must have been apprehended; for that which is not apprehended cannot be comprehended as a sentence. Therefore, this is not a restriction.

Nor is this injunction intended for one who desires knowledge of the meaning; therefore, let that which is valid remain valid, and let that which is invalid remain invalid. True, it is as stated by Pitṛmata: "That very validity is understood as being unrelated to an object to be accomplished (kārya).
What follows from this? From this, it follows that the Veda has no purpose consisting of an object to be accomplished.

But is it not the case that there is also a purpose consisting of an effect? No; because it is not preceded by an effect. For an object that is itself not an effect serves as the cause for an object that is an effect. And this has already been demonstrated: "It is said that Rudra wept."
Therefore, it must be wept by another as well. Consequently, the validity arising from that [Veda] depends upon other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*);
thus, its very independence (*anapekṣatva*) is undermined.
But surely this was set forth by the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*) for the sake of establishing that validity; why then is it [discussed] elsewhere?

It is led [to that conclusion]. True. What is being demonstrated is the syntactic unity of the established with the goal to be established; and it is precisely this that is being shown: that within such a syntactic unity, there is no purpose consisting of an action to be performed (*kārya*).
How then is this text to be understood? Is it by means of ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*)? What of this text? This is its [meaning]:
its lack of authority does not arise from its being a single syntactical unit with something that is not to be done, but rather from its being a single syntactical unit with what is to be done.

It has been stated that when there is a multiplicity of statements, this matter is inconceivable; yet in this case as well, you are ignorant of the meaning. Here, this very point is being challenged: for it is not possible to determine an obligation (*kartavyatā*) merely from the pursuit of an already established fact—as in this very instance: can crying and so forth actually be performed?

Is it not so that they cannot be [established] because of impossibility, and not because of following from what is already established? For it was precisely as something already established (*siddha*) that impossibility was stated; since an established thing depends on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and such a thing is impossible here, as has been accepted [on page b011].

Because a related object of knowledge (*prameya*) such as a cow and so forth is impossible; that is to say, because there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend Rudra’s connection with the separation from a desired object and so forth.
And thus he demonstrates the absence of another means of valid cognition:
"For [it is not the case that one could do so] by cutting out one's own omentum (*vapā*) and then [offering] that omentum..."
"Once it has been struck down, a sacrifice can be performed with a barren goat that has arisen [from it].
If, even here, the impossibility [of the sacrifice] follows simply from the established sequence, then why is there the introduction of a subordinate sentence within the great sentence?

Why then has this impossibility not been demonstrated by following the established conclusion? The answer is: even in the case of formulating an intermediate sentence, we are not released from this established conclusion. It is said: [we are] released.

This is the intended meaning. Intermediate sentences are introduced in order to demonstrate invalidity in every respect: for if one relies on the great sentence exactly as it is heard, there is still a contradiction with established doctrine; and if one relies even on an intermediate sentence not [explicitly] heard, there is likewise that same contradiction with established doctrine. Thus, because it is invalid in every way, this [is the case]. This very thing—
Invalidity is asserted on the basis of the established tradition [of Mīmāṃsā]: "Since the sacred tradition has action as its purpose, those parts which do not have that as their purpose are useless.
Here, an objection is raised: what is this specific designation, "those which do not have that as their purpose"?
He says in a single passage:
"But is it not the case that all the Veda now has no such purpose?
It has been stated that the entire [Veda] has no purpose consisting of an action to be performed. [For example: "To the spring, the kapiñjala birds..."
If it is argued that because one does not perform the *ālambhana* (the ritual killing), there is no following of the established rule (*siddhānugama*), [we reply]:
in the case of "one performs the *ālambhana* of *kapiñjala* birds for Vasanta," the meaning is established.

Because there is no [other] purpose for going, this is solely for the sake of the effect (*kāryārtham eva*); it is for the sake of the effect. Therefore, in order to exclude that [possibility], the specific qualification "of those whose meaning is already established" (*avadhṛtārthānām*) is stated. The objector says: "It follows! This very point has arrived: that this matter is inconceivable (*acintanīya*)."

If something were for the sake of what is to be done and something else were for the sake of what is not to be done, then this section (adhikaraṇa) would not need to be commenced; for the proposition that "the Vedic injunction is the defining characteristic" is established even by taking as its object that which is exclusively for the sake of what is to be done.

[Objection: "But if, due to the absence of conformity with an established fact (*siddhārtha*), sentences such as 'one should sacrifice three *kapiñjala* birds' are considered purposeless (*ānarthakya*) and thus beyond consideration, then let them be so; however, this does not mean that there is conformity with an established fact. It cannot be understood—or stated—that sentences regarding *kapiñjala* birds and the like possess conformity with an established fact. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even sentences regarding *kapiñjala* birds and the like do not have a purely prescriptive purpose (*kāryārthatva*); for even they [are connected] with an established fact (*siddhārtha*)."
Because they are sentences:
"He consecrates the Kapiñjala birds for Vasantā"—these are injunctions of subsidiaries (*aṅga-vidhi*). And injunctions of subsidiaries [belong to] the primary...

[The subordinate elements] have attained syntactic unity with the injunction; and the primary injunction itself has attained syntactic unity with a statement whose meaning is already established (*siddhārtha*). Thus, for all [the Vedas], there exists indeed a word—whether directly attaining syntactic unity or contained within another injunction—that possesses a meaning already established. Therefore, since the entire collection of words constitutes the Veda, it follows that the whole of it has a non-productive (*akārya*) meaning. Consequently, nothing is determined as being excluded by the phrase "of those things which do not have that [injunction] as their purpose."
The respondent said: It is determined that, because sentences have both established and things-to-be-established as their objects, this objection is raised by way of the established object.

In order to illuminate that very form by which this implication (*ākṣepa*) occurs, it was stated "of those things which do not have that as their meaning" (*atadarthānām*); it was not, however, for the purpose of excluding anything. Therefore, this was said: "the pointlessness of those things which do not have that as their meaning. And just as the implication arises through dependence upon an established meaning (*siddhārtha*), so too has it been explained.
And this has been explained by the author of the Bhāṣya: "Those [objections] are raised by way of an objection concerning one part.
One— [p.

For it is only when there is a state of being a single sentence (*vākyatva*) that the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) constitute parts of the injunctive words (*vādapada*). Otherwise, if they were independent, it would be impossible for them to be parts; for an independent entity cannot have parts. Thus, by employing the term "part" (*ekadeśa*), the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) has clarified that this objection is based on the assumption of a single sentence.

If this prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) relies on the assumption of a single sentence, then how is it that in the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) there is a question and answer regarding that very unity of sentence?

He asks: "What is your intention? For how can you say that the question and answer regarding syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) constitute the established conclusion (*siddhānta*"? The reply is: "This is my intention: this objection to validity (*prāmāṇya-ākṣepa*) is not based on syntactic unity."
But what is the status of those diverse statements that consist of explanatory eulogies (arthavāda)? What kind of description is it?

In the *pūrvapakṣa* of this deliberation, it was stated that [the passages] are purposeless because they do not have action as their purpose; here, in the *siddhānta*, it is declared that they possess purposefulness because they form a single syntactical unit with the eulogy.

For if the objection were based on the assumption of a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*), the resolution could not be achieved by resorting to that same assumption of a single syntactical unity; therefore, it is understood that the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is based on separate syntactical units, while the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is based on a single syntactical unity. He refutes this as follows:
"Ah! We have demonstrated the ignorant timidity of the Venerable One—namely, that those [objections] are being raised by way of refuting only a single part [of the whole].

This commentary is intended to demonstrate that this objection is based on the assumption of a single unified statement (*ekavākyatva*). Therefore, it is precisely by relying on the assumption of a single unified statement that this...

This is an objection to the authority of the entire Veda. However, as for the question and answer that occur in the *rāddhānta* (the final conclusion), those very points should be raised within the *rāddhānta* itself;
why are these questions and answers [placed] here? But what you, being anxious out of ignorance, have urged at the stage of the *pūrvapakṣa* (the prima facie argument)—that belongs to you alone.

It is merely cowardice. Furthermore, these questions and answers—concerning both what is to be avoided and what is to be established—will be addressed by us at the time of the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*).
Therefore, there is no room here for such an objection.
Furthermore, as for what was just now stated regarding the pointlessness [of the treatise] due to the diversity of examples, and because of the contradiction with what is seen in the scriptures,
and so forth—

The sūtras [are presented] for the purpose of elaborating upon the reasons for that prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa), in order to expand the arguments for the prima facie view. The purpose of this elaboration of reasons has been stated in the section concerning words (śabdādhikaraṇa).

All the arguments of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) must be set forth and then refuted; for if they were not set forth, some person of dull intellect might become agitated once again. In this regard, however, there is this further distinction: that [the objection] must be refuted by means of another refutation.

— Just as all possible reasons for [the eternity of] sound are refuted by the presentation of a single proposition (*pratijñā*), so too these reasons for futility (*ānarthakya*) do not require separate refutations, because they are to be refuted by various means. Therefore, they are presented individually in order to provide individual refutations.

"Therefore, it is said to be impermanent"—this is the Sūtra; however, this appears to be untenable. If, first of all, the impermanence of the sentence is being asserted, that is indeed agreed upon even by the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin). For "impermanent" is defined as having a cause; for whatever has a cause [is impermanent].

Therefore, it is impermanent. And a sentence consists of a collection of words, which are themselves composed of phonemes (varṇa) grasped in a specific sequence; because it possesses sequence as its cause, it is like that which has a cause. Now, one might object that such [a sequence] cannot be called impermanent because phonemes are eternal, and even if some word-meanings are impermanent, others—such as "cowness" (gotva)—are eternal. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Therefore, it is said to be impermanent."

In view of the fact that its purpose is already accomplished, the dependence upon other means of valid cognition constitutes its non-eternality; for both word and meaning are eternal in common worldly usage as well as in the Veda.
For this very reason, the author of the Bhāṣya has also explained this point: "Even though eternal things do not perform an eternal function.
What, then, is the function of an eternal thing? It is the cognition of its own object independently of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
This is the refutation. Therefore, it is precisely its independence from other means of valid cognition that is called "eternity.
Consequently, this objection is directed against that very point: "Therefore, it is said to be non-eternal.
"By means of the injunction; because it forms a single syntactical unit with the statement of the injunction. To what does this commentary refer?

Regarding the phrase "by means of an injunction" (*vidhinā*): is it not the case that an injunction (*vidhi*) cannot logically be the subject of an injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*)? True; it is spoken of by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Why is there figurative indication? Because of the statement, "due to being a single syntactical unit" (*ekavākyatvāt*).
Being a single syntactical unit with an injunction is not possible [if the injunction were the subject]. For indeed, everything constitutes a single syntactical unit precisely with the injunction.
Truth consists in being connected with that which ought to be done (*kartavyatā*). Now, it is not understood that praise itself is what ought to be done;
rather, it is connected with that which is praised. Is it then the case that the meaning of the injunction is not to be praised?
We do not say that it is not to be praised. However, qualities such as "being swiftest" produce praise for that which is enjoined.

These very [words] are implied by the phrase "of those not having that as their meaning"; and this sūtra is for the purpose of resolving that objection. Therefore, metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is appropriate. And for this very reason, how can there be syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*)?
Thus is the question:

what is this? This is the state of being a single syntactical unit with the statement of an injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*). And because the statement of the injunction is not a single syntactical unit with that [prohibition], there is no comprehension of it as something to be performed; and when there is comprehension of it as something not to be performed, [the injunction] does not exist.

[This concerns] validity. Therefore, this question arises: "How is there syntactical unity? The other replies: "It has been stated that [it is achieved] by means of the injunctive portion. But if this is so, does it not follow that the meaning is already established (*siddhārthatā*), rather than being something to be accomplished (*kāryārthatā*)? What is meant by "the meaning is already established, rather than being something to be accomplished"?
It has been stated that [the Veda] is not perceived as having a purpose consisting of an action (*kārya*). From what, then, does the understanding of its purposiveness as an action arise?
We reply: from the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*). Do not say this; for this specific connection is not intended to be expressed.
"One desiring prosperity should sacrifice" means "one should sacrifice, for from that [sacrifice] comes prosperity.
What is stated by this? That the comprehension of what is to be done does not arise merely from the statement of the injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*). What then?
We say it arises from the words of praise (*saṃstuti*). Thus it has been said: "These two meanings are distinct."

What is the intended meaning? This is the intended meaning: there might be comprehension of the action from the injunctive statement alone, provided that the comprehension were of a single form, as it would be from a word accompanied by a laudatory passage or from the word alone. But here, it is understood in a different form. "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice" is one means of comprehension; [and] "one should sacrifice... [is another].
Since prosperity arises from that [cause], this is yet another [instance]. And how could this person know the pointlessness of those things which do not have that as their purpose?

If it is asked, "For what purpose is there praise?"—then, since the understanding of the effect is the same [in both cases], why resort to another means? And how is it that this is another means? Who is to be blamed here, and by whom has this [other means] been resorted to?

And by what has it been produced? However, it is understood from the word alone. For when multiple words are employed, it is not observed that the comprehension of the meaning occurs independently of the other words. This has been demonstrated as follows: "The cloth becomes red; the cloth..."
Thus it is said: "It exists. No comprehension is observed from two words that are independent of the word *rakta* (red).
This very [comprehension] is the innate power (*autpattikī śakti*).
[Page 23] But surely, since it could be established even without that [reason], the objection regarding its pointlessness has been raised once again.
True; this reproach is directed at the speaker, not the cognizer; and it has already been stated that there can be no cognition without those [means].
And we are its practitioners, not its authors; it has been stated that there is no author for the Veda.
But surely, even though these are words of praise, an injunction is intended because the preceding passage has the form of an injunction?

It might be so; [but] it would not be intended that there is a connection with words of praise—what is the objection raised here? This is the objection raised here: Is there no syntactical connection within the subordinate sentence? For for one who maintains that the meaning is the connection between word-meanings, this is certainly not a different matter.

And if there is no difference in meaning, [the understanding of the action] is already established. It is not the case that the comprehension of the action fails to arise from intermediate syntactic connection (*avāntarānvaya*). Once the meanings of all the words have been understood, how can it be imagined that intermediate syntactic connection serves as the cause? Therefore, the comprehension of the action is caused solely by the syntactic connection of all the words and their meanings.
It cannot have as its cause an intermediate positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
[Objection: But surely we shall understand the injunction from that which is independent [of such concomitance].
What is this that has been stated without being stated?
This very thing has been stated without being stated.
But surely, even the intermediate syntactic connection (*avāntarānvaya*) has been accepted as a causal condition (*nimitta*).

[Objection: "It has been accepted by you. What is the fault? [Response: "Indeed, this is the fault; even here, that cannot be denied. [Objection: "True, for what is perceived cannot be denied, but not what is unperceived. [Response: "And there is no dual comprehension here, because it would entail the fallacy of sentence-splitting (*vākyabheda*)."

Thus it has been said. Now, as for what was stated—that neither an action (*kriyā*) nor anything connected with an action is understood—surely the state of being something to be done (*kartavyatā*) is not understood from the words of praise. And as for that state of being something to be done...
If it were to establish [something], it would lack the status of being Vedic.
And by whom was its Vedic status asserted? For this is indeed the Veda, since it is from this that the state of being a duty (kartavyatā) is understood.

It has been stated that from this [Veda], the sense of what is to be done (*kartavyatā*) is understood, and this objection regarding its authority (*prāmāṇya*) has been raised; and that very objection has now been resolved. What is the use here of [insisting on] its being Vedic? But if this were so, would not even the injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) be non-Vedic? For that too, in its comprehension...

The occasion (nimitta) is indeed that very Veda itself; certainly so in its capacity as an occasion, but not in its capacity as the thing occasioned (naimittika). The distinction is that the meaning of the word of praise is solely the occasion.
And the oral tradition is the same.

One might occasionally entertain this suspicion: that the words of the *arthavāda* were interpolated for the sake of praising the injunction (*vidhi*) and for the purpose of inducing the activity of the ignorant. That is incorrect;
for the traditional transmission is the same [in both cases]. No one at all remembers an interpolation of the *arthavāda* passages.

It has been stated that there is no difference in comprehension between these cases and that of injunctions (*vidhi*). If this is so, then the objection regarding the impossibility of weeping has been refuted;
on the contrary, this defect exists in the case of understanding something as a task to be accomplished (*kārya*), but not in the case of understanding an already established fact (*siddha-artha*).

But if this were the case, then in the instances where the words of an *arthavāda* terminate merely in a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), another means of knowledge would have to be sought for the comprehension of the praise; yet no such thing exists, as for example when *avakā* grasses are enjoined and water is praised.
Thus, there is the statement, "O fair-toothed one, she weeps. This applies everywhere in the case of thieves and so forth.

Therefore, once again, it is simply untenable. This is not untenable; for when there is syntactic unity with an injunctive purpose, it should be explained in such a way that the connection is understood through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As it has been said:
"But it is a figurative statement" (guṇavāda). The refutation of the accumulation of reasons, however, is to be understood in the same manner as the refutation of the reasons themselves.
[page 30] [page 31] [page 32]
Or it may be an injunction, because it conveys something not previously known; for a mere statement would be purposeless.

It has been stated that statements concerning established facts possess authority by virtue of their conveying a purposeful meaning. But how is it in a case where only a duty is understood, yet there is syntactic unity with another duty? For example: "The sacrificial post is made of Udumbara wood."
Thus: "The udumbara is indeed strength (ūrj), and cattle are strength; by means of strength he obtains strength and cattle for him, for the sake of securing strength.
From this, the relationship of means and end is understood between the sacrificial post and the udumbara, as well as between the cattle and the udumbara.
And syntactic unity is understood, because it is said: "Since cattle are accomplished by means of the udumbara wood, therefore the sacrificial post (yūpa) should be made of udumbara.

What is appropriate here? When the comprehension of that which is to be accomplished (sādhya) is possible, the comprehension of that which is already established (siddha) is not appropriate. Why? Because the sentence has the purpose of an injunction (vidhi), and an injunction requires something to be accomplished; furthermore, when the primary meaning is possible, a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is not appropriate.
But surely, two things to be proven cannot coexist within a single sentence. We too say exactly this; therefore, these two meanings are perceived here without any basis.
[Page 37] But is it not observed that even when multiple things are to be conveyed, a single sentence-unity (*ekavākyatā*) occurs,
as in such worldly sentences as "Devadatta, buy a cow," and so forth? This is not comparable.
For in that case (the *arthavāda*), the determination of the sentence's meaning is based on the force of the sense; here, however, it must be understood from the word itself.
Therefore, it is difficult to establish the authority of those [passages] that could be injunctions as being for the purpose of praise.
To this it is replied: But its status as a supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa) has already been stated.
It has been said that this is true, yet it is not tenable;
for it has also been stated that both are understood as things to be established. What is this contradictory prattle?

For there is no connection between two things simply because they are equal, as in the case of two qualities that are both to be accomplished (*sādhya*). How, then, is there the comprehension of a single object? If such comprehension exists, a corresponding cause must be postulated. But surely two things to be accomplished are perceived? In that case, there is no comprehension of a single object.

And this [usage] exists: "Since from this, that comes to be, therefore one should do this by means of this. In that case, it follows that the meaning of the word *bhavati* (it comes to be) is already established. How can there be the designation *bhavati* for that which is already established?

In this case, it is the establishment [of the object] by means of another instrument of knowledge that is required, not its establishment through the object itself. Whether already established or yet to be established, what is cognized by another instrument of knowledge serves as the cause for the comprehension of a different object. Therefore, because they share a single object, validity is established here as well.
And in some cases, an injunction is purposeless.

But was it not already stated in the preceding section that because an injunction is impossible, the Arthavādas terminate merely as authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); whereas here, it was suspected that they possess the status of objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and that suspicion was refuted? Why, then, is it now said that "an injunction is useless in some cases"?

Since it is possible for an injunction (*vidhi*) to have purposefulness, why is it stated merely on the basis of authority that "an injunction is sometimes purposeless"? [The answer is: "Because of its similarity to that. What is this "similarity to that"? It is precisely the possibility of an injunction that has been demonstrated here, not its impossibility.
This objection is based on a misconception of the facts.
Even here, by one who sets forth two things to be proven, it is not understood that the purpose of the injunction is for the sake of praise.

Thus it has been said. Where a praise is understood that is unconnected with the injunction, there it cannot be said that [the word] is for the purpose of praise. This is what is stated: "And in some cases the injunction would be purposeless.
For indeed...
The praise "the waters are submissive to the Vetasa" is appropriate; however, an injunction such as "they are born in the waters" is not possible.

Nevertheless, because a single meaning is understood, the status of being a cause (nimittatva) is postulated; it should be understood in this way here as well. This is the general principle: "and [it applies] when it is possible within the context."

[Page 42] What has been proposed by this? This is what has been proposed: when a single purpose is possible, it is not proper to assume multiple purposes, because that would contradict the means of application (*viniyoga*).

The enjoining agent, which depends solely upon application (*viniyoga*), cannot be made otherwise due to the difference in application; if it were otherwise, it would follow that there is a human-authored fabrication. Furthermore, even from another injunction (*vidhi*), the sentence—

A distinction follows. What has occurred? There is a sublation (*bādha*) of the understanding of a single purpose. Let it be sublated; however, an injunction (*niyoga*) ought not to sublate an application (*viniyoga*). For those who know sublation consider sublation to occur through the nature of the task (*kārya*).

Therefore, although two things to be proven (*sādhya*) are understood from the perspective of the entity (*vastutaḥ*), it is established that the comprehension of a single object occurs precisely because [the other] is already proven as a matter of valid cognition (*pramāṇataḥ*).
Thus, validity (*pramāṇatva*) remains even in such cases.
Or rather, there may be a logical reason (*hetu*), because of the establishment of its meaningfulness.
What, then, is the suspicion of invalidity here?

Whether the meaning of the word *hetu* (reason) is the instrument (*karaṇa*), or whether it is the meaning of the word *śūrpa* (winnowing basket), in either case, the meaning of the sentence consists of the mutually connected word-meanings.

For when a word-meaning lacks a logical connection (*ananvayin*), it is a mere mental flash (*pratibhā-mātra*) appearing either as a cause (*nimitta*) or as its effect (*naimittika*); therefore, it lacks authority (*aprāmāṇya*), but not when there is a connection (*anvayin*). Consequently, how can this [flash of intuition] fall within the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Nor is it reasonable to posit a different object (*arthāntara*) here.
Because there is no logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) and because it would not be relevant to the context (*anaupodghātika*).

But surely this consequence does exist: "Why is this not an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)? True, it exists; however, it would be purposeless. But surely this is its purpose: that if it were an *arthavāda*, the oblation (*homa*) would have to be performed with the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) alone.

[Page 46] "Otherwise, there would be no fixed rule. True, this purpose exists; however, this belongs to the third chapter (*tārtīya*). Furthermore, that which is prompted by another definition cannot be considered incidental (*prāsaṅgika*). This has already been considered.
In such passages as "This is the *nivīta* for humans," it must be stated that this [usage] falls within the scope of the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This is what is being said: for if it were a case of a logical reason (*hetu*), its status as an instrument (*karaṇatva*) would be understood as being based on that [reason]. If...

If it is argued that its status as Vedic is established by the Veda itself, [we reply: True, it is established; however, it is dependent. And if it is dependent, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be sought. Since such a means does not exist, [the claim] is a mere illusion. Therefore, it now functions as a logical reason (*hetu*). This is a reason because a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is possible through its being an effect. It is not...
It can be said that [the syntactical connection] culminates in the mere means of accomplishment (*pramāṇa*), because the connection exists for the sake of the result.
But is it not the case that the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) cannot be the instrument for producing food? For it is not the most effective means of accomplishment (*asādhakatama*).

Furthermore, because that which is occupied elsewhere does not perform [the action], the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is indeed possible through relativity. For the intention to speak is relative, and those who know the grammatical factors (*kāraka*) maintain that the factors arise from the speaker's intention. Those who know time have stated that its existence in the present tense is likewise merely relative. Therefore, this establishment of its meaningfulness is logically consistent.
...as "bhyām". Furthermore, this status of being an instrument (*karaṇa*) must necessarily be understood as relative; for it is the same even in the case of praise (*stuti*).
As for praise, however, because it is preceded by the word, there is no injunction (*codanā*) regarding it.
To this, it is replied: "This is not..."
It is the reason (*hetu*). Why? Because in the case of the *śūrpa* (winnowing basket) offering, it is understood as a reason. Furthermore, a reason must be something already established;
it cannot be understood as something yet to be proven. And the understanding that the offering is to be accomplished is derived from the Veda.

Furthermore, that which is understood as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) does not become dependent upon other means of knowledge on account of the Veda; therefore, this [Veda] is not a cause (*hetu*), just like a [logical] reason. And having established it thus, even though it is not present, it can be apprehended as being present.

But has it not been stated that the present itself does not exist? By whom was it said that it does not exist? It is established that an undertaking which culminates in a result receives the designation "present. However, this is not tenable under the view that [the action] is yet to be performed (*vidhi-pakṣa*). For it is impossible to determine its application to anything other than the actual object.
Furthermore, the relative nature of the instrument can be established only within my own position;
for in the position of an injunction, by what could its status as a distinct action be prevented?

If it is argued that [the function] follows from the word *śūrpa* (winnowing basket), then ladles (*darvī*), cooking pots (*pithara*), and so forth are excluded; furthermore, the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) becomes contradicted. Therefore, it was said: "And if the reason were to persist, [it would apply] to the winnowing basket alone because of the specific instruction. If it is argued that there is no contradiction of the reason, [we reply: there would be a lack of restriction (*avyavasthā*).
In that case, the very same reason for non-establishment is contradiction (*vyāghāta*), because there is no object to be negated.
Even in the absence of an object to be negated, a causal factor (*kāraka-hetu*) attains its own existence, just as a signifying factor (*jñāpaka-hetu*) does. Therefore, like a cause—
The *gadas* also exist solely as authoritative means of knowledge,
because they are treatises on their subject matter.

As for what was stated— that "its purpose is indeed seen to be the comprehension of ritual action"— that is incorrect; for in the case of the mantras, the purpose of the Vedic study would be unintended.

How is it that the meaning is not intended to be expressed? This is demonstrated by nine reasons, beginning with contradiction by a scriptural statement whose purpose is that very meaning. But surely, if the meaning is not intended to be expressed, then the scriptural statements and so forth whose purpose is that meaning must themselves also have their meanings unintended.

It is said: "Oṃ. How then can it be that they (the mantras) have an unintended meaning? Because of mutual contradiction—the very fact of having unconnected meanings is the cause for the meaning being unintended. If the mantras have unintended meanings, then the instructional texts (*śāstra*) concerning their meaning would also have unintended meanings; this is a mutual contradiction. [This applies] when there is an intention to denote the *raśanā* (rope).
There would be a contradiction of that *arthavāda* rule which states, "He takes up the horse's bridle. And yet...
It has been demonstrated that contradiction can be avoided through enumeration and other such means.
But the meaning of the sentence remains undifferentiated. To this it is replied: its meaning is not unintended.

Self-study (*svādhyāya*). The purposefulness of self-study has been stated by virtue of its connection to the injunction (*niyoga*), because it is declared to be an authority regarding what is to be done (*kārya*), even when it is employed for the sake of another through its denotation of that which is to be done.

What is this "application" (*prayoga*)? It means performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). When it is understood that a statement has the intended meaning because it is useful for the purpose being performed, it cannot be set aside by the "explanatory passages" (*tadarthaśāstra*) and other such factors. Indeed, sentences are seen that merely restate what is already established, such as: "He who, knowing thus, performs the Full Moon sacrifice."

[Page b062] Such passages as these do not have other meanings, as has been demonstrated through specific features such as the injunctions regarding deities (*devatā-vidhāna*) and so forth. This should be understood in the same way for every sūtra.
Furthermore,
the validity of this point is supported by Vedic indicative marks (*liṅga*) as well, such as: "One worships the Āgnīdhra altar with a verse addressed to Agni."
Thus, and so forth.
This concludes the second quarter of the first chapter in the *Bṛhatī*.
Now begins the third quarter:
"Because Dharma has its root in the Word, that which is not based on the Word should be disregarded."
—Why is this irrelevant matter being considered? What is irrelevant? It is the investigation into matters that are not based on Vedic injunction (*codanā*). And [the Sūtra] states:
"Since Dharma has the Word as its sole source, that which is not based on the Word should be disregarded. If it is not based on the Word...

It has been asserted; and the consideration of what is unasserted undermines the assertion. Furthermore, due to the contradiction between the preceding and the following, it follows that [the position] was not preceded by conscious deliberation. Now, if this is the intended meaning—that even this [was taught] by those who know the Vedas—

"It has been accepted as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, this too must be investigated. This is incorrect. For even perception and the other [means of knowledge] have been accepted by them as means of valid cognition; those, too, would consequently have to be investigated. But surely—

This has been examined. Where was it examined? In the context of the sūtra "When there is contact with the existent, for persons... as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Is that sūtra intended to resolve the doubt as to whether perception is a valid means of knowledge or not? No; its purpose is solely to show that it is not a valid means of knowledge with respect to *dharma*.
[The opponent says: "Then the Sūtra has not been considered as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in this treatise.
Therefore, that which was promised (*pratijñāta*) should be considered, but not that which was merely accepted (*abhyupagata*) and not promised, such as the Smṛti-śāstra."

Therefore, this inquiry is irrelevant. To this it is replied: this inquiry concerns the subject matter of the proposition (*pratijñā*). But surely that proposition has as its object independent words, and here there is no independence. True; there is no independence.
This inquiry concerns only those words that are *svatantra* (independent). Is the word "aṣṭakā" an independent word?
It is not an independent word; rather, it is connected to an independent word. By which independent word is this [connected]?

What is the connection? It is the phrase, "which people welcome. What follows from that? Because it is dependent upon and subordinate to something else, this [Smṛti] also attains the status of a means of proof (*sādhaka*), and by virtue of its similarity to that, the others do so as well. This is what he states: "Since Dharma has the Word as its source, that which is not based on the Word would be unreliable (*anapekṣa*)."
And this is required by such passages as "which people welcome," and so forth; therefore, these [qualities] are indeed not explicitly stated by words.
That very point of the thesis is raised again: it has been stated that identity of purpose between that which is dependent and that which is independent is impossible because their objects differ.
But surely, in this case, a difference in object is not possible, since both have the effect as their purpose.
For it is precisely that which is said not to be possible. But surely there will be an inference based on the effect itself; the reason for abandoning that must be stated.

But surely, even the comprehension of the effect cannot be abandoned; therefore, who can prevent the inference established by that sequence? True, it cannot be prevented, provided there were no misconception regarding memory in this case.

What fault is there in the conceit of recollection? [If you say it is that] from recollection inference would follow, and not from the effect [of the object], what follows from that? For recollection has the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as its object, not the external object itself. Why is this so? Because the cognition of the object is preceded by that [recollection]. [Objection:
Then its status as a valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) is established. [Reply: We say no, because it is possible even when it does not correspond to reality (*ayathārthatva*).

Therefore, the establishment of inference does not proceed from an effect—this being our inference. Nor is this [inference] possible for us through the intervention of memory; for the effect is not related to memory, but rather related to its cause.

Therefore, it is not independent because that [cognition] does not exist for something separated [from its cause]; thus, this effect is equivalent to the recollection of the son of a barren woman. But surely, even "not being the first time" (*anidampathamata*) is seen to be a cause for such a state—as in the comprehension of the meaning of words, such as "this is the Veda" or "this is a Brāhmaṇa. This is an unequal comparison.

In the case of an object already perceived, it is logical that there is no "firstness" (anidamparatā), for in that instance, the very perception of the object constitutes the root [of knowledge]. But here, that [perception] is absent; therefore, another means of valid cognition must be sought in this matter.

And it has been stated that there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that [Veda]. Therefore, dharma is not characterized by anything other than Vedic injunction (*codanā*). Alternatively, because of the commonality of the agent, inference (*anumāna*) may be a means of valid cognition; it is not [otherwise].

The Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for when a means of valid cognition is such (i.e., true), its very nature is comprehension. When it is not in accordance with reality, however, there is a defective cause and a misconception (*viparyaya*). Now, this comprehension indeed exists, and yet there is no misconception.

But surely, due to the absence of a cause, there is the concomitance of defective causality; can it be said that there is an absence of a cause? Why can it not be said? Because the connection with the Veda is possible.
True, one cannot say there is an absence of a cause; nor indeed can one say there is its presence.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the existence of the cause is understood solely from the effect? [Reply: No; for it has been stated that there is an intervention by memory and so forth. What is this "intervention by memory"? This is it: for in this case, memory is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [Page b074]

It is perceived by that [cognition]. What follows from this? Only the validity residing in that [cognition] can be inferred, not the validity residing in the word. For the inference of the capacity of a perceived cause is made from its effect, not of an unperceived one. But surely, since remembrance itself is not possible, there must be an inference of another cause; of what [is it the cause]?
[Objection: Of the effect. [Reply: Do not say so; it has already been stated that recollection is not the cause.
[Objection: In that case, there is an inference of another cause for the recollection. [Reply: What does this have to do with the effect? For one thing cannot have another as its cause.

It must be so. But surely it will occur through an indirect succession (*praṇāḍyā*). In that case, the effect is to be known from its cause, but not the cause from its effect; for the effect terminates in the mere cause and does not depend upon a succession from it.
Indeed, the accomplishment of the cause is the reason for the production of the effect, not even that which accomplishes it [the effect]. [There is] no connection—

Furthermore, in the case of inference, there would result a lack of definitive certainty. But surely, an effect that has a restricted cause also makes known the cause of that cause? Not so; for in that case, only that much [is known].
The reason is as follows: Is it the case that in this effect, memory is merely the cause of the cause of the word?
Yes, it is so stated; however, in that case, it follows that even the veneration of shrines (*caityavandana*) and similar acts would possess validity (*prāmāṇya*).

If it is argued that this is not so because [the cause] is not admitted [as such], then there can be no inference of a specific cause from its effect; therefore, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be sought. And it has already been stated that such a means does not exist.
Thus, like the recollection of the son of a barren woman, this [recollection] is without a basis and cannot function as a means of cognition.

Therefore, it is precisely the defectiveness of the cause that is established here; consequently, the *codanā* lacks authoritative validity (*aprāmāṇya*). Ah! You are one who does not understand the principles of logic. Why is this? Because of the effect—

To that extent, there is the capacity for recollection. Now, since this recollection is without a cause, its causelessness is determined regarding the recollection. Yet, that causelessness cannot be determined regarding the recollection, because the connection with the Veda is possible, and no other cause for this effect is possible.
Because [such things as] the veneration of caityas and so forth are impossible [in that context], our inference based on effect is not [applicable]. Therefore—

The non-apprehension of the tantra refers to its textual subject matter; furthermore, it is possible for the learner to forget it. Therefore, the independence of the *codanā* (Vedic injunction) remains unimpaired. As for that which was further stated: "That which people welcome..."

Thus, the claim that "the mantras have the *aṣṭakā* as their indicative mark" is untenable. Why? Because it was already stated that they lack authority precisely because they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with that [injunction]. How then can that very same thing be put forward as a reason for their authority?

This is not presented as a reason for its authoritative status; rather, it is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) insofar as a connection with the Veda is possible. How so? It is an indicative mark because the mention of the deity in the ritual action depends upon that indicative mark. Therefore, by restating the deity derived from the words of the mantra (*māntravarṇikī*), it strengthens the connection with the Veda. As for what was further stated—that those [mantras] which have a perceptible purpose...
"From that very [source]"—this which was said is incorrect. What is it here that was said to be incorrect? Indeed, it was said to be exceedingly incorrect.
It implies that the injunction for study depends upon other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Or rather, by whom has its own nature been denied?

[The Vedic injunction] has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), just like the act of threshing and so forth. How then, in the subsequent section (*adhikaraṇa*), is there a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) due to having a visible purpose? We shall explain that specific point in that very place.
But when there is a contradiction, [the Smṛti] should be disregarded; for when there is no [contradiction], it is an inference [of a Vedic basis].

If it is possible that, upon contact with the Veda, there occurs an unimpeded inference from the effect in the case of tradition (smṛti), then the authority of the Veda [is established], while its lack of authority [in the case of tradition] is also [demonstrated].

By this very reasoning, it follows [that the Smṛti is invalid]. How so? Because of contradiction. And a contradiction with the Smṛti is indeed perceived in the Veda. Furthermore, when there is a contradiction, there is a lack of authority due to mutual conflict, as in the case of the total wrapping of the *audumbarī* post versus the touching of it. This is true, provided that the action is inferred from something else.
There would be no contradiction. Why from anything else? Precisely from the contrary Vedic word itself;
for when a matter is directly established by the Veda, a human statement that contradicts it and depends on other factors cannot be an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is a means of valid cognition only when it does not sublate another means of valid cognition, but not even when it is sublated by such a one. For the Naiyāyikas maintain that there is a contradiction (*bādha*) between what is already established and what is yet to be proven; that which is established does not sublate that which is to be proven, but rather, that which is to be proven is sublated by that which is established. And this Vedic matter is already established, because its cause is apprehended through perception.
Inference that has a contradictory cause as its object gains no validity for itself, just like the inference of coldness in fire.

Therefore, there is no authoritative status for tradition (*smṛti*) when it is in contradiction [with direct perception]. Because of its lack of authority, there is no contradiction; and because there is no contradiction, there is no sublation.

And because it is unimpeded, the authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) remains unrefuted. But surely, if the word has an action as its object, what contradiction is there? For when two actions are perceived—even if they pertain to a single purpose—they may be performed alternatively.

They do not dare to contradict one another; for when a contradiction is perceived regarding an entity that has been established as possessing its own true nature (*satattva*), it produces a mutual conflict within consciousness. However, an effect cannot be apprehended as a unity, because it is understood through its very distinctions, such as its specific adjuncts (*anubandha*) and so forth. And an effect with distinct adjuncts does not bring about a contradiction in its essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Furthermore, because they serve a single purpose, there is merely a contradiction regarding simultaneous performance; for the performance of a ritual action is [only] possible once its nature is fully known, and this contradiction in performance is resolved by means of option (*vikalpa*), since the purpose is accomplished through incidental application (*prasaṅga*). Therefore, there is no contradiction here at all, as the word has the purpose of conveying the action. Why, then, is this lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) being suspected?
And it is refuted:
this would indeed be true if there were no contradiction in action when there is a contradiction in performance. But has this not already been stated?

[The opponent says: "Even when there is a contradiction regarding the performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) in the case of the *vṛhadrathantara* and other such [sāmans], no contradiction regarding the task (*kārya*) arises.

[The author replies: You are ignorant of optional (*vaikalpika*) ritual elements; for it is precisely the performance that is called the "task. To say that there is no contradiction regarding the task when there is a contradiction regarding that [performance] is mere idle chatter.

How, then, can there be repeated performance by many? Because the task is understood in that very same way. In that case, there is a contradiction between the injunctions "one should sacrifice with rice" and "one should sacrifice with barley. Very well; how then is there validity?
It has been stated: "because of independence. But what will this independence accomplish regarding validity when there is a contradiction?
For contradiction brings about a mutual reversal, and such a reversal would establish the lack of validity as the crowned head [of the argument].

True, this is so; however, in this case, the reversal itself cannot even find its own footing, because both [the cognition and its object] are independent. It is not [the case that they are dependent].
In that case, there is a contradiction. How is there no contradiction? Because the performance is one, due to the single word.
Is this like a Mahendra-illusion? This is so because the scripture is one; and thus, from the perception of contradiction, it is exactly as stated.

But memory is not like that. Why? Because the identity [of the object] is not established. For in that case, the cause is inferential; and as has been stated, when the opponent [the object] persists, inference does not find a footing for itself.
Therefore, the charge of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*) is refuted here, whereas it applies to the other [case]; thus there is a difference. Therefore, memory—

The opening objection regarding the lack of authority for the Vedic injunction (*codanā*)— on the grounds that it has causes perceivable through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— is refuted by the rejection of inference. As it has been said:
"And because of the perception of the cause. What is the meaning of "or it is a separate topical section" (*adhikaraṇāntaram*)?
This is the meaning: the statement of a reason that is independent of the previous reasoning; it is a reason that requires another reason.
This has been stated previously. Here, however, being stated independently, it is called a separate topic (*adhikaraṇāntara*).
But how can there be the observation of a reason independent of other arguments when there is a contradiction with the inference from effect (*kāryānumāna*)? [The reason is: the reason—

Simply from observation. For when a cause is already perceived, the inference of another cause does not proceed. In this case, greed alone is the perceived cause. Therefore, when a cause is perceived, neither a Vedic inference that is contradictory nor one that is non-contradictory can arise. In the absence of a Vedic inference, there would be no Vedic application of perceived causes.
Is there such a thing as being an object of apprehension? Let there be; but where, then, is the designation of "invalidity" (aprāmāṇya) useful?
[p. b092] It is useful for establishing a distinction between objects: those whose assistance is unperceived are not apprehended, whereas those whose purpose is perceived are apprehended. Therefore—
[The action] has a visible purpose. It is logical to declare its lack of authority on the grounds that it serves a visible cause. As it has been said:
"The gift of the cloth used in the *vaisarjana* oblation has a visible purpose.
[Objection: "If it is argued that this is not contradicted because it does not conflict with the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*)."
The authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is established by resolving contradictions and non-contradictions. This very contradiction— where it exists and where it does not—
is now the subject at hand.
It is considered for the purpose of rejection and acquisition. For what purpose is the demonstration of the pervasion of the object?
This treatise is indeed intent upon stating the nature of the *nyāya* (method of reasoning), not upon being restricted to the definition of the subject matter (*lakṣya*). True, as you have said.
This very statement of the nature of the *nyāya* is demonstrated through the pervasion of its objects; for even when the nature of the *nyāya* has been stated, [it remains to be shown] in which...

In the domain of consciousness, it appears as if non-existent to those whose intellects are focused on effects; therefore, this effort has been made by those of perfected wisdom to dispel that [misconception]. For instance, in this very example, there is one who considers there to be a contradiction regarding the sequence and time [of the process].

The rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) and other such acts appear to be contradictory. How so? It has been established in the section on *krama* (sequence) that the performance of a ritual act must follow the meaning of the text as it is heard, according to the expansion of the injunctions. Here, there is a contradiction because of opposition to the expansion of the direct injunctions (*pratyakṣavidhivitāna*).

To this it is replied: there is a contradiction only if there were a contradiction with the meaning of the scripture (*śāstra*). And it has been stated in the second aphorism that the scripture is for the sake of what is to be accomplished (*kārya*), not for the sake of an elaborate exposition of injunctions (*vidhi*); for it is only the eternally extended *kārya* that is perceived.

Because the canopy is dependent upon its effect, it does not possess the status of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*) independently; and there is no contradiction between one effect and another effect, because [the latter] is subordinate to the former rather than being a distinct category of entity (*padārtha*). How is this so with respect to time?
For time, too, is an accumulation of effects; therefore, due to its dependence upon those [effects], it is not contradictory.

"Moreover, sequence occurs at a later time for objects that have already been attained; when the objects are being attained, there is no sequence at all. What has he stated here that was not already stated? He...
For in this way, the subordinate status of sequence has been established; and since that has already been stated, it need not be established again.
However, there is an underlying intention here: namely, that sequence and time are not merely the accumulation of a series.
[The opponent] thinks: How so? [If one were to say,] "One should sacrifice with the Full-moon sacrifice on the full-moon day," what accumulation (*pracaya*) of rites would there be here?
Since this applies equally to the second and subsequent [Full-moon sacrifices], it is not logical for that accumulation to possess the status of being the "Full-moon sacrifice" (*paurṇamāsītva*).
Furthermore, the understanding of sequence is observed through the nature of the task (*kāryatayā*), as in: "The Adhvaryu, having initiated the Gṛhapati... and so forth.
Therefore, a resolution by way of being a quality is not tenable; for there is a contradiction between being an effect and being a cause.

This is answered as follows: Is the canopy for initiation understood as a subordinate element (*dīkṣāvitāna*) when the duty of initiation has already been established by the sentence "The Adhvaryu [initiates] the householder"? Or is this understood as an independent duty to be performed on its own, without dependence on that prior establishment, like the *samidh* offerings and so forth? For there can be no duty without a duty-bearer (*adhikārin*).
If the extension of the effect is understood through inference, it cannot be understood as being a separate effect;
therefore, since the extension is not understood when the effect itself is not understood, with what could there be a contradiction?
What, then, is the scope of the statement "the Adhvaryu [chooses] the Gṛhapati"? We shall explain this on its own occasion. This same [principle] applies to time as well.
The rebuttal: How so? What is intended by your venerable self when you mention the word "Paurṇamāsī"?
Even there, it is simply a collection of actions arising from conjunctions and disjunctions of the cups (grahas). This, however, is the distinction: [it is] a collection of the effects as enjoined.

The constituent part is in one place; the accumulation of other actions occurs elsewhere. In that regard, there is no contradiction due to the accumulation of other actions. However, the accumulation of enjoined effects occurs at a time subsequent to the action itself.
Therefore, there is no contradiction, just as in the case of sequential order.
"And acts such as sipping water do not constitute an interruption," thus [it is said] regarding each constituent part of the ritual action.

[This refers to] the *prāya*. For it is only when a ritual act (*padārtha*) together with its auxiliary elements (*sāṅga*) is present that its sequence relative to another ritual act is understood. Therefore, Vedic performances must be understood as being necessarily conjoined with acts such as sipping water (*ācamana*).
Since no contradiction is perceived among them, the disagreement would be equal.

When there is such disagreement regarding the meaning of words, how could the Veda lack authority? [It would lack authority] because of doubt and the resulting failure to reach a definitive understanding.
But is it not the case that this lack of authority has already been cited under the rule *sandigdheṣu vākyaśeṣāt*? True, it has been cited.

However, in cases where the status of being a cause for a meaning is universally established through its very multiplicity of referents—as in the case of words such as *akṣa*—there may be doubt arising from usage. But where, due to conflicting opinions (*vipratipatti*), the causality of a particular sense is only occasionally established, there no doubt arises from usage.

[It] occurs. And the remainder of the sentence removes doubt regarding the application (*prayoga*), not doubt regarding the denotation (*abhidhāna*). This doubt pertains to the denotation, and the doubt regarding the denotation pertains to linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*).
[This occurs] through disagreement (*vipratipatti*). It has been stated that the knowledge of the meaning of the Veda is rooted in the linguistic usage of words and their meanings.

Therefore, just as in linguistic usage, disagreement is found to exist regarding the meaning of the Veda as well. Nor can this disagreement be rejected on the grounds of contradiction with the meaning of the Veda, because the sense of a sentence admits of both possibilities. Therefore...

Due to a misconception regarding the characteristic mark (*nimitta*), there is no ascertainment (*anadhyavasāya*); and due to the lack of ascertainment, there is invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*). Or rather, those who abide by the treatise (*śāstra*) [are authoritative], because that [treatise] is the cause of it.

It is true that there would be no contradiction if it were so; however, contradiction is indeed understood from the very nature of the effects. For it is heard in such supplementary passages (vākyaśeṣas) as, "The cows run after the boar," and so forth. What follows from this? [That they are] caused by specific conditions.
That which is understood [is as follows]: "But surely it follows that the determination is made from the remainder of the sentence (vākyaśeṣa). This does not follow at all;

for in that case, the determination occurs when there is a cause of doubt. Here, however, it is precisely the opposite that is being refuted: namely, that the boar and so forth alone are the primary [meaning] by virtue of their inherent nature (*autpattika*), and not the black bird and so forth.

[Page b102] But surely, it must be admitted that the understanding of the cause [of dharma] comes from the Veda alone, and not from worldly usage, as is the case with sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) and the like. If this is so, what is the fault? Indeed, there is none.
There is another fault: for that very status of having the Veda as its source is not established.

Why? Because as long as the status of having worldly sources is not understood, it cannot be understood from the Veda. Therefore, we do not speak of "Vedic-ness," but rather of the usage by the learned (śiṣṭa).

Thus, it is called "powerful" (*balavān*) in accordance with the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*). And since its innate nature (*autpattikatva*) is established, no cognition contrary to that [innateness] can find a place for itself in the case of Prayāga. Innate...

For by that [secondary usage], linguistic practice (*vyavahāra*) is established even through figurative application (*gauṇa*). If, indeed, the assumption of the innate nature (*autpattikatva*) of both were derived solely from linguistic practice, then there would be a contradiction in that assumption due to mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). In this case, however, it has been stated that the innate nature of the scriptural usage is established from another source. And once that is established, the opposing view—
A contradiction is understood because it conflicts with inference. Therefore, the conventional usage of meaning is not figurative.
However, that which is enjoined should be accepted as valid, since it is not contradicted by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If this non-Aryan usage is thus secondary (*gauṇa*), then those words which are not well-known as having a basis (*nimitta*) in Aryan usage must likewise lack a basis in Vedic usage, such as *pika*, *nema*, *sata*, *tāmara-sa*, and so forth.

If it is argued that this should not be so, then it follows that this very [Vedic word] lacks authority. If it is argued that the comprehension of the meaning occurs by virtue of grammar, etymology, and so forth, we say no; for those two are rooted in actual usage.
How, then, is there the inference of the meanings of stems and suffixes? It is by virtue of their application (*viniyoga*).

The inference of stems and suffixes follows established causes as recognized in the linguistic usage of the elders for a mantra that has been applied and for an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) that serves as a supplement to the sentence; it cannot, however, constitute an injunctive statement (*vidhyuddeśa*) based on words whose meaning is to be inferred.
Therefore, the Vedic injunction lacks authority;
this is true, provided that the inference based on general observation contradicts the inference from the effect.

But if, precisely where the opponent exists, there is a contradiction with the inference of the matter, then who can prevent that which has its counter-position destroyed? Furthermore, what is the reason that it is not a "generally observed" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) [inference]? It would simply not be a "general" [property] if its counter-position were not established. Therefore, even that which is established by the practice of barbarians (*mleccha*) that lacks a counter-position [is valid].

The sign (nimitta) alone is the means for understanding the meaning of the Veda. Therefore, the independence of the injunction (*codanā*) remains established, its contrary positions having been refuted by the consideration of contradiction and non-contradiction.

If it is argued that [the Veda] is a treatise on practice (*prayogaśāstra*), then what is the reason for suspecting that what is already established lacks independence due to being a human product? It is suspected both from the perspective of its being an effect and from the perspective of its being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As for the effect: [The text continues: "The Veda is not a treatise on practice, because it does not prescribe the performance of actions; for a treatise on practice is that which prescribes the performance of actions, such as the *Kalpasūtras*. Furthermore, the Veda is not a treatise on practice because it teaches things that are not to be performed, such as the creation of the world and so forth. And so on. Regarding the means of valid cognition: "The Veda is not a means of valid cognition, because it is composed by a person; for whatever is composed by a person is not a means of valid cognition, like the works of Kālidāsa and others. And so on. Thus, the doubt arises from both the nature of the effect and the nature of the means of valid cognition. Therefore, the author states: "Because it is an effect... and so forth. This is the meaning. Now, he provides the formal proof (*sādhana*) for this: "And because it is a human composition... and so forth. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates the accumulation of reasons. The phrase "because it is a human composition" is the reason (*hetu*). The phrase "like the works of Kālidāsa and others" is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). The word "and" (*ca*) implies the application (*upanaya*) and the conclusion (*nigamana*). The word "this" (*tat*) refers to the Veda. The word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) indicates the summary of the reason. The word "hence" (*ataḥ*) indicates the summary of the conclusion. The word "thus" (*iti*) indicates the end of the formal proof. Now, he anticipates an objection: "But if the Veda were a human composition, how could it be a means of valid cognition? To this he replies: "It is not so, because there is no contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition. That is to say, even if the Veda were a human composition, it would still be a means of valid cognition, provided there is no contradiction with perception and the other means of valid cognition. For example, just as the words of a reliable person (*āptavākya*) are a means of valid cognition despite being a human composition, so too is the Veda. Therefore, there is no fault. Now, he anticipates another objection: "But if the Veda were a human composition, how could it be independent? To this he replies: "Even if it were a human composition, it would be independent because it is not dependent on anything else. That is to say, even if the Veda were a human composition, it would be independent because it does not depend on any other means of valid cognition. For example, just as the words of a reliable person are independent despite being a human composition, so too is the Veda. Therefore, there is no fault. Now, he anticipates another objection: "But if the Veda were a human composition, how could it be eternal? To this he replies: "Even if it were a human composition, it would be eternal because it is not subject to destruction. That is to say, even if the Veda were a human composition, it would be eternal because it is not subject to destruction. For example, just as space (*ākāśa*) is eternal despite being a human composition [in the sense of being a convention], so too is the Veda. Therefore, there is no fault. Now, he anticipates another objection: "But if the Veda were a human composition, how could it be authoritative? To this he replies: "Even if it were a human composition, it would be authoritative because it is free from defects. That is to say, even if the Veda were a human composition, it would be authoritative because it is free from defects such as error, deceit, and the like. For example, just as the words of a reliable person are authoritative despite being a human composition, so too is the Veda. Therefore, there is no fault. Now, he anticipates another objection: "But if the Veda were a human composition, how could it be a means of valid cognition regarding supersensible objects? To this he replies: "Even if it were a human composition, it would be a means of valid cognition regarding supersensible objects because it is based on the authority of those who have direct knowledge of them. That is to say, even if the Veda were a human composition, it would be a means of valid cognition regarding supersensible objects because it is based on the authority of those who have direct knowledge of those objects. For example, just as the words of a reliable person regarding supersensible matters are a means of valid cognition despite being a human composition, so too is the Veda. Therefore, there is no fault. Now, he anticipates another objection: "But if the Veda were a human composition, how could it be free from error? To this he replies: "Even if it were a human composition, it would be free from error because it is consistent with the teachings of the omniscient ones. That is to say, even if the Veda were a human composition, it would be free from error because it is consistent with the teachings of the omniscient ones. For example, just as the words of a reliable person are free from error despite being a human composition, so too is the Veda. Therefore, there is no fault. Now, he anticipates another objection: "But if the Veda were a human composition, how could it be the source of all knowledge? To this he replies: "Even if it were a human composition, it would be the source of all knowledge because it contains all things within its scope. That is to say, even if the Veda were a human composition, it would be the source of all knowledge because it encompasses all objects of knowledge. For example, just as a great ocean is the source of all waters despite being a human composition [in the sense of being a natural phenomenon], so too is the Veda. Therefore, there is no fault. Now, he anticipates another objection: "But if the Veda were a human composition, how could it be the ultimate authority? To this he replies: "Even if it were a human composition, it would be the ultimate authority because it is not superseded by any other means of valid cognition. That is to say, even if the Veda were a human composition, it would be the ultimate authority because it is not contradicted by perception, inference, or other means of valid cognition. For example, just as the words of a reliable person are the ultimate authority despite being a human composition, so too is the Veda. Therefore, there is no fault. Now, he anticipates another objection: "But if the Veda were a human composition, how could it be the path to liberation? To this he replies: "Even if it were a human composition, it would be the path to liberation because it teaches the means to liberation. That is to say, even if the Veda were a human composition, it would be the path to liberation because it correctly teaches the means to attain liberation. For example, just as the instructions of a reliable physician lead to health despite being a human composition, so too is the Veda. Therefore, there is no fault. Now, he anticipates another objection: "But if the Veda were a human composition, how could it be the source of dharma? To this he replies: "Even if it were a human composition, it would be the source of dharma because it is the basis for the knowledge of dharma. That is to say, even if the Veda were a human composition, it would be the source of dharma because it is the foundation for understanding what is to be done and what is to be avoided.
