For example, just as the law codes of Manu and others are sources of dharma despite being human compositions, so too is the Veda. Therefore, there is no fault. Now, he anticipates another objection: "But if the Veda were a human composition, how could it be eternal? To this he replies: "Even if it were a human composition, it would be eternal because its essence is unchanging. That is to say, even if the Veda were a human composition, it would be eternal because its fundamental nature remains constant. For example, just as the sun is eternal despite its daily rising and setting, so too is the Veda. Therefore, there is no fault. Now, he anticipates another objection: "But if the Veda were a human composition, how could it be the beginningless source of tradition? To this he replies: "Even if it were a human composition, it would be the beginningless source of tradition because it has been handed down through an unbroken lineage of teachers. That is to say, even if the Veda were a human composition, it would be the beginningless source of tradition because it has been transmitted through a continuous succession of teachers and students. For example, just as the tradition of grammar is beginningless despite being a human composition, so too is the Veda. Therefore, there is no fault. Now, he anticipates another objection: "But if the Veda were a human composition, how could it be the supreme authority? To

The recitation of what has been studied is like [the recitation from] another branch (śākhā); furthermore, the authority [of the Veda] is the word of the Teacher, for "the word of the Teacher is authoritative.

Now, is it not contradictory that it be both of human origin and independent? What here is contradictory? Things exist exactly as they are understood. And in this case, two things are understood: its being of human origin and its independence.

[The opponent argues: "From the fact of being remembered, there is human authorship; from the words concerning its effect, there is independence. Therefore, let both [authorship and independence] exist.
[Reply:
No, because there is no restriction regarding what is non-existent.
This is untenable: that it is both of human origin and independent.
Its status as being of human origin is established; it is not something to be excluded from the category of "recitation" (pravacana) like the *Kāṭhaka* and other such texts.
Furthermore, "composition" (*kṛti*) is defined as the expression of an object perceived through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not merely the production of phonemes and the like.

Therefore, there is dependence. As for the argument presented—that the recitation of what has been studied is like that of another *śākhā*—this is not equal to another *śākhā*; for the practice of performance is understood as being accessible through the ritual action itself, for the purpose of the rules regarding accents and the like.
Because of this abandonment, it brings about the non-interruption of the meanings of the words when one proceeds to their immediate practice.
And since these meanings, being perceived without interruption, are easily performed, this is the purpose of the recitation of what has been studied.
[This is] not [the case] for the Teachers (Ācāryas). For this very reason, it is designated as a *prayogaśāstra* (treatise on performance), being denoted by the term *kalpa*;

for here there is a "constructing" (*kalpanā*) of ritual items, but not their being something to be enjoined (*vidheya*). Just as with a gem, there is the "determination" (*klṛpti*) of what has already been understood. As it has been said: "The word of the Teacher is authoritative"—it is understood from that very authority.

This is not so; for this statement lacks authority. It has been stated that a word possesses independence with respect to its own form (*svarūpa*), but not with respect to its function (*kārya*). Therefore, because this sentence is subordinate to something else, it lacks authority.

An explanation following what has been observed is appropriate; or rather, the Veda is intended as the teacher (*ācārya*), or else it is by relying on that which is authoritative, namely the word of the teacher. What, then, is the purpose of this deliberation? Since this treatise is devoted to the formulation of injunctions, we perceive no contradiction.
In this regard, there exists a conception that contradicts what has been prescribed: namely, the conception that the Darśapūrṇamāsa and other rites are to be performed on all lunar days (tithis).
This conception is contradicted by the scriptural hearing of specific times; and what is contradictory is not to be accepted.
For otherwise, due to the conflict with that [specific time], the injunction would lose its authoritative status because of the resulting contradiction.

Because it is established by means of inference, that which is connected to it would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Here, there is an example of both an object that is established and one that is not established. What is this "established object" and what is "not established"?

And why? Because those who possess the conceit of being Easterners, Northerners, or Southerners perform this or that [practice]. This restriction applies only to the *holākā* and similar rites. Furthermore, since there is nothing to regulate such conceit, there would be no fixed rule.

But how, then, is there no determiner? First of all, the injunction (*vidhi*) is not a determiner, for it terminates merely in the act of enjoining (*niyoga*). Nor is the word "rite" (*karman*), such as *holākā* and so forth, a determiner of [the specific rite].

Because of the mention of specific distinctions. And there is nothing else—neither quality (*guṇa*), genus (*jāti*), configuration (*saṃsthāna*), nor location (*deśa*)—since those are absent. Nor indeed is there a designation (*samākhyā*). [Objection: But surely, one who is born in a certain place is designated by that region, as in "Easterners," "Northerners," or "Southerners. [Response: This designation does not arise from birth alone, for it also applies to those who have merely come from such places.

Because they are equal, the name (*samākhyā*) is not a restrictive factor; however, terms such as *lohitākṣa* (red-eyed) are invariably restrictive. Furthermore, what is the utility of this inquiry for the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*)?

Does such singleness exist? Or how could it not exist? No; whether there is a determining factor or not, what does that matter to the claim of independence? This very thing has arisen: there is a misconception.
And since no basis for it is found, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers it to be invalid.

In the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, it is resolved that Vedic speech does not originate from conceit (*abhimāna*). If Vedic speech were to originate from conceit, then there would be a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) in the injunction (*codanā*), as well as in conceit itself.
Let it be that this overweening pride is unreal because its basis does not exist; however, one cannot claim that the Vedic injunction itself is unreal.
Because there would be no treatise on the production of linguistic usage, there would be no fixed rule regarding words.
But how so?
If, due to the non-recollection of grammar, the Veda were to be rendered rootless, would its lack of authority be suspected?

If words such as *gāvī* and others were also of beginningless existence, what would happen to the *codanā* (Vedic injunction)? It is said in reply: [this would apply] to words such as *aśvagoṇī* and others.
Those who know the Veda remember that it has a fixed meaning, and because its meaning is fixed, they also provide an interpretation.

And if grammar were a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then this [conclusion] would be established. For if it were rootless, the determination of specific meanings would lack any basis in authority. Let it be so; what harm is there to us? It follows that the meaning of the Veda would have indeterminate causes, and consequently, due to the resulting uncertainty, it would lack authority. Nor can the principle applicable to those who stand within the [Vedic] scriptures be invoked here.

To say this: therefore, the determination here is based solely on grammatical convention (*vyākaraṇa*). Consequently, its justification must be investigated. This is what is being examined: Is the beginninglessness of words such as "cow" (*go*) due to the dewlap and so forth?
And regarding the statement that "the words *gāvī* and so forth have a beginning," this is investigated: does this tradition (*smṛti*) possess a valid source (*mūla*), or not?

What, then, is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Let the consideration of its source be set aside for a moment; first, the grammatical instruction (*śabdānuśāsana*) itself has an indefinite meaning.

What is this "uncertainty of meaning"? This uncertainty of meaning arises because this treatise is intended for the regulation of usage (*prayoga-niyama*), yet that usage cannot be regulated [by the treatise]. If, on the other hand, the regulation is established through usage alone, then it follows that words such as *gāvī* and so forth are also beginningless (*anādi*) with respect to the animal possessing a dewlap and other characteristics.

[Page b120] But how, moreover, is the application [of the rule] not possible to restrict? It is not possible in this way: first of all, this is the instruction—that suffixes occur after a verbal root (*dhātu*). And thus, some—

Some [hold that the suffixes occur] in the agentive case, some in the objective case, and some in all kārakas except for the agent; yet all of this is untenable. How is it untenable? It is untenable in this way: it is stated, "of the verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*); what indeed is this "verbal root"?

[Page b121] Now, one might object: having recited certain words in a particular sequence according to the rule "bhū-vādayo dhātavaḥ" (the words beginning with *bhū* are verbal roots), they are designated as "verbal roots."

Thus, the designation [saṃjñā] has been established. Therefore, why would it not follow that suffixes occur after those things which are designated by that designation? [If so,] the correctness of forms such as *gaṇḍati* and the like would result, as well as *ghaṭaṃ bhūyate*. Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of a third-case suffix (*tārtīyapratyaya*) being applied even to *sattā* and other such [abstract] entities.
If it is argued that this reading is not of Vedic origin (*anārṣa*), let this be the rebuttal; however, as for words such as *gaṇḍati* and the like, they simply do not occur at all in usage.

Now, if it is said that a verbal root (*dhātu*) is that which expresses action, no; for there would be no application of such words as *bhavati* (he exists) and *tiṣṭhati* (he stands), and the recitation of the root *gaṇḍ* would be meaningless. If it is argued that even a non-action is sometimes perceived [as the meaning of a root], [then we reply:]...

In that case, the restriction arises from the application (*prayoga*), not from the action (*kriyā*). If it is argued that the mere presence of the cognition of the action is the restrictor, we have already stated that a cognition of equality between superimposition (*adhyāropa*) and non-superimposition (*anadhyāropa*) is impossible. Therefore, this too is not a restrictor. If it is argued that the restriction arises from both the recitation (*pāṭha*) and the statement of the action (*kriyāvacana*), [we reply:]...

In that case as well, it must be stated whether [the word] is taken collectively or distributively. If it is taken collectively, then *gaṇḍati*, *bhavati*, and so forth would be excluded in exactly the same way. If it is taken distributively, then the recitation of *pacati* and so forth would be purposeless.

If it is argued that this is for the purpose of excluding roots such as *ā-gam* (to come), then both [the inclusion and exclusion] have been resorted to. This being the case, the same fault remains regarding roots such as *bhū*. Therefore, once again, usage alone is the refuge.

Likewise, the restriction of the *kāraka*s is not established. According to the rule "that which is fixed (*dhruva*) in relation to departure is the *apādāna*," the *apādāna* is defined by its state of being fixed.
However, it is not possible for that which is fixed to be a *kāraka* at all. In the case of "one ram moves away from another ram," [the latter] is a *kāraka*.
Of what action is this "from the ram" (*meṣāt*) the *kāraka*? For that which [is the agent] in a particular action—
That which possesses activity (*vyāpāra*) with respect to that [action] is a causal factor (*kāraka*). Furthermore, no activity is perceived in that which is stationary.

Now, if the intention is that activity is perceived in the caravan and the chariot because [the person] has fallen from the caravan and the chariot, there is no such activity in the caravan or the chariot; rather, it is of the nature of movement.

Furthermore, a factor of action (*kāraka*) engaged in one activity cannot simultaneously be a factor in another activity. Nor is it possible to determine that the agent of the root *gam* (to go) is the same as the one who "cooks" (*pacati*). Therefore, for one who asserts that a factor of action is devoid of activity, it follows that what is currently active is something other than the factor.

Everything would be a factor (*kāraka*) everywhere. In the case of "he cooks" (*pacati*), there would be the same application [of the term] as in "he recites," "he runs," or "he eats. Likewise, in cases such as "he cooks," the agent (*kartṛ*) would be the recipient (*sampradāna*) for "he recites" and so forth. This is another rule regarding factors: "That person whom one intends through the object (*karman*) is the recipient (*sampradāna*)."

If it is intended by the object (*karman*), then it is not the agent (*kāraka*). For we know from the example "he gives a cow to the teacher" (*upādhyāyāya gāṃ dadāti*) that "that which is intended by the agent through the object is the recipient (*sampradāna*"). Furthermore, an *kāraka* is an operation that is not produced apart from the operation of the agent; however, in the case of that which is intended [as the recipient], there is no [operation] in its being intended.
Because of the designation of "it" as both the object (*karman*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*) by that activity, the fruit becomes the object, not a factor of action (*kāraka*),
just as heaven is the object of the sacrifice.
But is it not the case that, according to the rule "that which one intends by means of an action [is called the object]," the *kāraka* (participant) is understood as the object (*karman*)?
In that case, there would be all the more reason for it to lack the status of a *kāraka*; for a designation as a *kāraka* does not occur merely through a connection with other *kārakas*.

Because the term *kāraka* is derived from the sense of "one who acts" (*karoti*), it is therefore not possible to understand the restriction of *kārakas* through the treatise (*śāstra*). Furthermore, if *kārakatva* were based on a connection with an action, a specific grammatical instruction would not be established.

Moreover, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) would apply to all *kārakas*, and there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that heaven (*svarga*) is a *kāraka* of the sacrifice, as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings.

If it is argued that there is a restriction regarding the primary materials (*jāti*) in the New and Full Moon sacrifices based on their performance and realization, then that restriction does not arise from scripture. Furthermore, when it is said that "the most effective means is the instrument" (*karaṇa*), what constitutes this "most effective means"?
If it is argued that [the instrument] is that after whose operation the accomplishment of the action occurs, then it follows that rice is the instrument for the preparation of cooked rice.
Or, if its status as the "most effective means" (*sādhakatama*) is established by some other reason, that must be stated. If you say it is because of its abundance (*prācurya*), then one must ask:
whose activity (*vyāpāra*) recurs again and again until the completion of the result? For who does not possess such activity? It remains [to be explained].

The cooker is ready, equipped with the collection of vessels and other implements; in that case, one would necessarily say "he cooks with wood" or "he cooks in the pot with water. If you accept this, then there would be no fixed rule for usage such as "he cooks rice in a pot with wood. If you argue that it depends on actual usage, then homage to the grammatical treatise!

The grammatical rule states that "the locus (ādhāra) is the substratum (adhikaraṇa). Of what is it the locus? That in which something is placed is the locus. If, however, it were the action itself, there would be the undesirable consequence that all the factors of action (kārakas) would be loci.

Now, if it is argued that "that which possesses the action is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*)," then [the rule] would not apply to the expression "he cooks on level ground," whereas it would apply to "he cooks in water. Furthermore, "he eats on a mat" would be a corruption (*apabhraṃśa*), for that is the locus of the agent, not of the action, nor of the object. If it is argued that it is "where all the case-factors (*kāraka*) are established," then [it applies to] the pot—

Otherwise, the expression "he cooks the cooking" (*modanaṃ pacati*) would be untenable; or else, it would follow that the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) itself becomes a grammatical factor (*kāraka*). For it cannot be said that a locus is "situated in a locus. Alternatively, it has been stated that the cause for being a locus is the state of being a locus for all factors by virtue of being related [to them], and furthermore, the lack of activity (*nirvyāpāratva*)—as in the case of time and so forth—is [also a factor].
This has been stated. As for what is also said—that "the object is that which is most desired by the agent"—what is this superlative?
Everything is most desired for the sake of action. Now, if the intention is this: that which the action is for the sake of is indicated by the superlative suffix (*tamap*).

It is maintained that [the object] has attained the status of being a non-agent (*akārakatva*). For it is stated in the *Saṃpradāna-sūtra*: "And likewise, that which is not desired (*anīpsita*) when so connected. If it is asked, "In what way is it connected? and one replies, "By means of the sense of the superlative suffix *-tama*," then it cannot be said to be "not desired," because no other thing superior to it has been mentioned. Therefore, this is merely a blind statement.

And what has not been stated is indeed already implied. Therefore, we understand that everything must be established through reasoning alone (*prayoga*), and not from the treatise (*śāstra*). Likewise, regarding the statement "the agent is independent" (*svatantraḥ kartā*): what is this independence?
It is activity proceeding from one's own will (*icchā*).

[If it were so,] one would incur the state of being a non-agent in such cases as "he is born," "he dies," or "the bank falls"; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of the word being grammatically incorrect.
Now, if you consider another factor to be dependent upon that [activity], what is this dependence?

That which is produced when something else exists is dependent upon it. In that case, it follows that all factors would possess the status of the agent (kartṛtva), because they are mutually dependent; for we do not perceive the production of anything whatsoever without [the presence of] something else. Of that which...

For that without which the accomplishment of an operation does not occur, it does not depend upon that; yet the collection of causal factors (*kāraka*) is mutually dependent, therefore there is no fixed rule.
If it is argued that the agent is that whose operation is conveyed by the verbal root (*dhātu*), we do not know whose [operation] is conveyed by the root.

Thus, because it is understood as being related to all [of them], we see such usage as "the pieces of wood cook" (*kāṣṭhāni pacanti*). If you say, "It belongs to that which one intends to speak of," then the cause for that intention must be stated. [Such] usage...

If this is argued, then the scripture (*śāstra*) is indeed the authority; therefore, this restriction of the agent based on the scripture is without foundation. That which is the "instigator" (*prayojaka*) is also explained by the same [rules] as the "instigated" (*prayojya*). Furthermore, those [terms] whose adjuncts are the meanings of the verbal roots (*arthopadopa*) are also restrictors by means of either a specific action or a specific meaning. For example:

Regarding the rule *rucyarthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ*, [the word *prīyamāṇa*] is used in the sense of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). Regarding the rule *bhītrārthānāṃ bhayahetuḥ*, it is used in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*). Here too, we do not know whether this [mention of the root *ruc*] is intended for the restriction of the recipient, or for the explicit mention of the meaning of *ruc*. What follows from this?
If it were merely the utterance of words meaning "to please," then [the rule] would not apply in the case of "modakas are to be given to Devadatta. Why?

Because those [words] have the sense of "pleasing" (ruci), since they are the cause of pleasure. But surely, when the sense of the verbal root is taken as having the meaning of "pleasing," is that [sense] without an object? It is not without an object; rather, whatever pleases someone, that is the object of the sense of "pleasing."

If it is argued that the utterance of the verbal root is based on the mention of the *modaka* (sweetmeat), then [the question] "Do the *modakas* please Devadatta? would be an improper response. If it is argued that the usage is made with reference to that very [root], we say no, because the question and answer would remain untenable.

This utterance is for the purpose of refuting the objection, not for the sake of establishing the grammatical correctness of the fourth case (*caturthī*) usage. Likewise, even in the case of the ablative (*apādāna*), the state of being a cause of fear establishes the status of the mere factor (*kāraka*) of fear as the ablative; it applies this to all factors—

Because fear arises from dependence on the activity of the poet; however, in the case of *upapada*s and the like, there is no status as a *kāraka* at all. By this very same line of reasoning, the prescription of case-endings (*vibhakti*) is also refuted, since the prescription of case-endings is preceded by the determination of the object (*viṣaya*). Thus, for a restriction that is preceded by the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, there is no sentence-meaning—

The state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) [belongs to time and so forth] because they are established through that [action], since they are understood from it. In this way, the *kṛt* suffixes have also been explained. The *tiṅ* suffixes as well have conditions such as time (*kāla*), but they do not denote those [conditions].
Furthermore, it is impossible to define a restriction when [the objects] are not perceived. And by whom was it said that time and so forth [are denoted]?

[Page b135] Why are they not mentioned? It has been stated by the Blessed One and by the author of the Bhāṣya that "the meaning of a verbal root (dhātvartha) is that which has already come into being.
Furthermore, it is not possible for the meaning of a verbal root to be defined solely by means of the meaning of a verbal root. The same applies to the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth.
Because the meaning of injunctions and the like cannot be determined.

But how is it that injunctions and the like cannot be determined? Because differentiation depends upon the force of the meanings of accompanying words (*upapada*); differentiation cannot be understood by itself. Furthermore, a restriction among those whose own meanings are non-different is difficult to state.

It is like the case of *aśvagoṇī* and similar compounds; likewise, the formation of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) and compounds (*samāsa*) is difficult to determine based on the rule concerning semantic competency (*samartha*).

What is this "rule concerning semantic competency"? It is the grammatical instruction: "From among semantically competent [words], [the suffix is added] after the first," and "A word-formation rule applies when there is semantic competency."

And semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) consists in the connection with a single referent. The specific designation of the compound and the specific designation of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) are for the purpose of defining that [competency]. And by means of those [designations], the two [types of semantic competency] are characterized.

The prescription of specific secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) involves mutual dependence. Likewise, the supplementary rule regarding compounds of non-coordinated meanings (*asamartha-samāsa*) and the fact that secondary derivatives do not arise from such [non-coordinated] meanings cannot be understood without actual usage. If that were so, the purpose of the treatise would be defeated. For instance, in the case of non-coordinated meanings, we have compounds such as *aśrāddhabhojī* ("one who does not eat at a funeral feast"), *dadhighaṭaḥ* ("a pot of curd"), and *gorathaḥ* ("an ox-cart"). And from coordinated meanings—

The derivation of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) occurs as in "he digs with his finger" (*aṅgulyā khanati*) or "come from the root of a tree" (*vṛkṣamūlād āgataḥ*). Therefore, the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) is a refuge for usage; it is not capable of restricting usage.

Likewise, in the rule "A meaningful element that is neither a root nor an affix is a nominal stem" (*arthavad adhātur apratyayaḥ prātipadikam*), it must be stated whether "meaningfulness" (*arthavattva*) is functional or innate. What, then, is the distinction? If meaningfulness were functional...

The statement "the relationship between word and meaning is established" does not hold. Furthermore, if that [relationship] were innate (*autpattika*), then because the scripture is merely a means for explaining it, the scripture's utility would not be established. For if this scripture is a means, it must have as its basis that which is to be attained (*upeya*); thus, there is a mutual dependence.
[The term *dhātu*] would thus lack its basis; and consequently, the application of accentual operations and suffixal rules conditioned by it would not be established.
Furthermore, the expression "not a root (*adhātu*) and not a suffix (*apratyaya*)" would result in a redundancy of its constituent parts.

What is excluded by this? It was stated for the purpose that even though the verbal root (*dhātu*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) possess meaning, they should not receive the designation of *prātipadika*. If, however, the designation of *prātipadika* were to apply to a sentence on the basis of its possessing a specific meaning, then [the rule] "that which is neither a root nor a suffix" would be contradicted.

If it is argued that the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) is for the purpose of excluding that [case], then the rule *adhātur apratyayaḥ* would be meaningless; for its exclusion would also follow from the mention of "compound. When there is a single meaning, that which excludes [the suffix] does not apply when there is a different meaning.

If this is argued, it is incorrect, because even a compound is accepted as having a distinct meaning, which renders the mention of the word "or" (*vā*) redundant. If, on the other hand, the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) is for the purpose of excluding meaningful aggregates (*arthavat-samudāya*), then the mention of "kṛt and taddhita [suffixes]" (*kṛttaddhita-grahaṇa*) should not have been made. For in that case as well, what is intended is precisely an aggregate consisting of that which ends in a *kṛt* suffix and that which ends in a *taddhita* suffix. Therefore...

First of all, it is difficult to establish that formal practice (*prayoga*) is a means [to knowledge]. And when the means itself is difficult to establish, the knowledge of the object to be attained (*upeya*) becomes utterly remote.

Furthermore, the examination of what has been stated, what has not been stated, and what has been poorly stated occurs for commentators precisely through the application of formal practice (*prayoga*).
It must be understood [in this way]. Furthermore, the specific statement regarding the Veda (*chandas*) would not be tenable if its purpose were unknown.

If it is argued that [the knowledge of the Veda] is preceded by such knowledge [of the auxiliary sciences], then [the Veda itself] would be useless; for the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) are employed for the sake of knowing the meaning of the Veda, and the meaning of the Veda is not for the sake of knowing the auxiliary sciences, since the latter exist for the sake of action (*kārya*). Therefore, of the word...

Instruction is indeed nothing but teaching. And thus, by demonstrating mutually contradictory meanings, the authors of the Prātiśākhyas and other treatises have clearly revealed the lack of fixed rule regarding the scriptures. Furthermore, this other point [p.

The statement of the commentators—that [a grammatical operation] does not occur because there is no formal application (aprayoga)—shows that the authors of the Sūtras lack full knowledge of the root [principle]. For one who does not fully know the root, the restriction based on their statement is indeed a restriction [only for them]. Furthermore, the mention of "classes" (ākṛtigaṇa) is the matrix (mātṛkā) for the restriction according to the treatise, as is the inclusion of the term "often" (bahula).

This is the drumbeat of unrestraint according to the treatises. Thus, by those who accept the beginninglessness of this tradition (*smṛti*), its own ignorance has been accepted. Therefore, by those who claim that knowledge of the Vedic meaning arises from an unascertained cause, the world following the true path has been deluded. Or rather, [this is due to] the straightforwardness manifested through faith. This very—

It has been stated [by Patañjali]: "Because there is no rule for the production of usage, there would be no fixed determination regarding words. Now, this objection was raised against the system of Pāṇini; however, we know the restrictive rule from another source.

No; this very same method of instruction applies to others as well. Let us set aside for a moment the question of whether sound is subject to error because it is produced through effort; rather, this alone is first to be investigated: does sound possess a beginning?
Is linguistic usage established or not? Why is it not established? It is not established in this way.

It has been stated that the establishment of the usage of words and their meanings occurs through an unbroken succession of the linguistic usage of the elders (*vṛddha*), and that succession is indeed uninterrupted.
And when there is no interruption, what room is there for corruption (*apabhraṃśa*)? At most, for whom would it serve to establish one's own personal usage?
Whether it be a name or a technical designation (*paribhāṣā*) that has been established, there is a recollection of its author, as is the case with this very grammar (*vyākaraṇa*). However,
no author of the relationship between words such as *gāvī* and their referents is remembered, in the same way as one is remembered for objects such as a jar (*ghaṭa*).

Therefore, there is no occasion for [the world] having a beginning. True, if there were no occasion; but such an occasion does exist, for it is observed that even when children intend to utter one word, they utter another—for instance, intending to say *kartā*, they say *kattā*, or intending to say *Viṣṇuḥ*, they say *viṇṇuḥ*. This is true.

In the case of children, a different pronunciation is observed; however, that is merely limited to their own linguistic usage. Furthermore, that which originates from memory is also produced by incapacity, and thus such a designation is indeed born of incapacity. To this, it is replied:

—“It is true that if we were to say that the status of being ‘unborn from incapacity’ (*aśaktija*) applies to words such as *gāvī* on the basis of their being observed to arise from incapacity, then we would be right. However, we have stated that, having perceived [the word] through memory, there is no possible source for that memory, based on the observation of its being ‘unborn from incapacity. But is this not exactly what was already said? No; for when stated in that manner, it constitutes an inference (*anumāna*). And in that case, there is the fallacy of the contradictory (*viruddha*), and so forth.”
[Page 145] This is the occasion.
Furthermore, it cannot be said that there is an absence of a basis for this traditional teaching (*smṛti*); by this much alone, one perceives an incapacity.
Moreover, an absence that merely negates possibility does not require the perception of an incapacity. Therefore—

It cannot be said that this recollection is otherwise [than valid]. If that is so, it has been stated that this is merely recollection and is not capable of establishing a restrictive rule (*niyama*); yet, it is indeed capable of establishing a restrictive rule. How, then, is it known that it is not [capable]? It is known from that very same explanation of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) and the non-pervader (*avyāpaka*) mentioned previously; such is that explanation.
In some way it has been explained by the commentators; however it has been explained, let it be accepted just so. For even that is indeed nothing but memory.

By doing so, one does not postulate a difference in the expressive power (*śakti*) of synonymous words with respect to a single meaning. For even today, it is observed that the cause of understanding a meaning for a given word is mediated by the recollection of another word, as in the case of *adritunnāṅgam* (‘one whose limbs were crushed by a mountain’). Precisely for this reason:

Grammarians accept the transposition of case endings; when it is said, "He has come from the Aśmakas," they understand it as "from the Aśmakas" (*aśmakebhyaḥ*). Therefore, even by this method, the authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) cannot be challenged.
Because there is no injunction for separate application, there is unity of purpose.
Is it indeed [the case that...

The purpose of this inquiry—whether the words used in common worldly usage are the same as those in the Veda, and whether their meanings are also the same—is as follows: Is this not, in fact, an introductory discussion (*upoddhāta*) for the section concerning the universal form (*ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*)? How so? If the words are the same and the meanings are the same, then [the question arises] regarding the denotation of the individual (*vyakti*).
The sublation of validity can be effected through the door of the word itself; if, however, the words were one thing and the objects another, then invalidity would follow simply from that difference—
so what is the point of presenting invalidity by way of asserting that the word denotes the individual?
Therefore, this was said: "This, first of all, must be examined.
How is there a suspicion of difference?
Because of the difference in designation; for learned authorities designate both worldly and Vedic [entities] as distinct.
They recite the word *agni* with the final nasal sound (*ṇatva*). Likewise, this is seen in such passages as "the gods [came] themselves" (*devāsaḥ svayam*).

Similarly, even a difference in meaning (*arthānyatva*) is perceived from the Veda itself, as in: "The divine cows indeed carry [the load] on their backs," "the golden-leaved tree," and "clarified butter is honey. But surely, in this way, the comprehension of the Vedic meaning would not be possible?

Since the meaning of the Veda is preceded by the worldly meanings of words, it was objected that [the Veda] might be exactly like that [worldly discourse]. [To this, it is replied: "In that case, the Veda would not be a means of valid cognition. We say: "Yes, it is so," for it does not conform to [human] purposes.

It ought to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If that is so, then we understand the purpose from the means of valid cognition itself. What is that means of valid cognition? It is the realization of the non-difference between the word and its meaning. For difference would have to exist either by way of essential nature (*svarūpa*) or by way of function (*kārya*). First, as for essential nature, it is simply that same thing consisting of the phonemes (*varṇa*), such as "cow" and so forth; and as for function, it is likewise that same thing.

[The opponent asks: "What is the cause for the cognition of that which possesses a dewlap and so forth? By what means do we perceive its difference? [The proponent replies: "Surely by means of the substitution of *ṇ* and so forth. [The opponent asks:

"But is that not a difference in phonemes (*varṇa*) and not a difference in the word (*pada*), since it is the cause for the cognition of the meaning? [The proponent replies: "That is true of that [specific case]."
And there is oneness.
151] But surely, because the meanings are different, the words must be different; for it is precisely the difference in meaning that remains unestablished.

Because the meaning "they carry while lying on their backs" is not established; nor can this meaning be understood from the word *uttāna* when there is a difference in referent. Therefore, due to the absence of both [the literal and the figurative], unity is established. How then is it that [it is said], "The divine cows indeed carry while lying on their backs"? It has been stated:

The authority [of the Veda] has been explained by means of figurative description (*guṇavāda*) for the purpose of praise. How, then, is the designation [of "authorless"] to be understood? It is intended to establish that the object of the instruction is not otherwise; [it is so designated] by virtue of being independent, as opposed to being dependent [on other means of knowledge].
The distinction of objects is established. There is an injunction for performance.
It has been stated that the collection [of words] is for the sake of action in relation to those things already existing.
This is now being investigated: we do not know whether this term "of the elements" (bhūtānām) refers to the generic form (ākṛti) of the elements or to the individual manifestation (vyakti).

[Objection: Is it not the case that whatever is cognized from something must be inherent in it? And both [the universal and the particular] are cognized from this [word]. How then can it be said that "because cognition occurs through the universal and because action is possible with respect to the individual"? Furthermore, what here is untenable? This is what is untenable here: [that the word applies] to the individual.

And because of the impossibility of action [in the case of the universal]. For it has been stated that the possibility of action is the reason for [the word] denoting the individual (*vyakti*). Has the cognition of the individual been refuted by this? Yes, it is said; because the cognition is declared to belong to the form (*ākṛti*).

[Page b154] For the "Beloved of the Gods" (devānāṃ priyaḥ) is indeed one who does not understand the treatises. What here is this lack of understanding of the treatises? This is the lack of understanding of the treatises here: it has been stated that "the collection [of the Veda] is for the purpose of action. And by virtue of being for the purpose of action...

The state of being "become that" (*tadbhūtatva*) has been defined. Since that which is not perceived cannot serve as the purpose of an action, this state of being "become that" exists only in the individual instance (*vyakti*). If it is then asked how there can be an understanding of the universal (*sāmānya*), it can only be said that [the universal] exists;
however, its state of being "become that" does not consist in its serving as the purpose of an action.

[Page 155] But surely, if there were an apprehension of the universal (*sāmānya*), the apprehension of the individual (*vyakti*) would not follow! Oh, what a lack of reflection even regarding experience! Of which universal is there an apprehension? For it is by way of being related—

A universal that is being cognized is not cognized as "universal," for the cognition of a related entity depends upon another related entity. Moreover, in this case, it is not cognized by way of being a form (*rūpa*) and its possessor (*rūpin*); indeed, there is no cognition of a form devoid of its possessor. If such were the case, the form itself would not exist. Why?

[Page 156] If that is so, why is there a presentation by way of distinction? It is for the purpose of demonstrating that the form (rūpa) does not cohere with the action (kriyā). And it is not logical for that which does not cohere to be the meaning of a word, just as in the case of "Bring the lion in the cage," where the cage [is not the object of the action].

[The opponent asks: "If [the universal] is not denoted, why then is it introduced? [The author replies: It is for the purpose of demonstrating this very point. For what purpose? To show that the proponent of the *ākṛti* (form) theory asserts a lack of authority [for the Veda] because the cause [of the word's application] is not connected [to the action].
However, in cases such as 'He sprinkles the rice-grains' (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), they maintain that the individual (*vyakti*) is what is connected [to the action]."

Or, even if one adopts the position that [the word] refers to the individual or its essence (*tadbhūta*), how is independence established? Whether it is established or not, the proponent of the universal (*jāti*) at least resorts to an improper method; however, in the case of the position that it refers to the individual, the postulation of the instrument (*karaṇa*) must conform to the effect (*kārya*).
It is logical. But how can this position be logical, since the tradition of usage among elders cannot be established as the cause for [linguistic] acquisition? Why can it not be so?
For the usage of elders is based upon positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and these two—positive and negative concomitance—[apply to] universals (*sāmānya*)...
These two are the basis [for linguistic usage]. Furthermore, we perceive no cause for the acquisition of linguistic proficiency other than the usage of the elders.
It has already been stated that this is because the author is not remembered.
But has not "being based on that" (*tadbhūtatva*) already been rejected even with respect to form (*ākṛti*), on the grounds that "the Veda has action as its purpose"?
Which of these two is stronger? We say: it is the *kārya* (the thing to be accomplished). For that is the seed of conceptualization for the entire cycle of causes;
together with usage among the elders and so forth, it is a cause by virtue of being "based on that," and [it is established] through its being an effect.
That state of being more deeply rooted is understood, and a corresponding etymological derivation must be postulated.

If that cannot be shown to be preceded by the usage of elders, then let it be postulated as either a convention (*samaya*), an artificiality (*kṛtakatva*), or a delusion (*vyāmoha*). But surely, comprehension from the usage of elders is observed in the case of children; for nothing is impossible when it is actually perceived.

[The opponent says: "It is called so. [The author replies: "In that case, it follows [that the name exists]! It is true that it follows from the perspective of conventional designation (*darśana*), but it does not follow from the perspective of the causal sign (*nimitta*).
Furthermore, neither the convention nor the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is perceived. Therefore, the conceptualization of a causal sign is indeed refuted by this reasoning."
It is observed as follows:

if, moreover, it is the individual substance itself, as characterized by a universal, that serves as the cause for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, then what fault would there be? None at all; indeed, there is no fault whatsoever, since it functions as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇatve*).

However, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be stated. Here, the very apprehension of the effect (*kāryapratipatti*) is the means of valid cognition. For the apprehension of the effect is not possible when the individual (*vyakti*) has not been apprehended. Indeed, a specific individual cannot be communicated if it is not characterized by its universal (*sāmānya*); thus, everything is logically consistent. Therefore, it is considered that the individual is denoted.

This has been demonstrated by Vyāḍi. For this very reason, it is logically established that numbers and the like possess both the status of being enjoined (*viniyojya*) and the status of being prescribed (*upādeya*).
Indeed, that which is not supported cannot partake in the connection with qualities; and thus there is the designation of its distinctness.

It is not tenable in the case of the genus; therefore, it should be understood that its "becoming that" (tadbhūtatā) is based solely on the individual. However, the configuration (ākṛti) [is denoted] because [the word] serves the purpose of action.
To this it is replied: even if this position were sometimes established, the comprehension of the effect is indeed inconclusive, as in the case of the *śyenacit* [altar].

Regarding the statement "one should pile," it cannot be said here that the word refers to an individual [or that it denotes the state of having become that]. For no action pertaining to an individual is perceived here. Why is it not perceived? Because this is not the meaning of the sentence:
"that which is piled by falcons is a 'falcon-pile' (śyenacit). This is because of the traditional rule (smṛti): "The term 'fire-altar' (agni) is applied when it is used as the name of an object."
And it has been stated that the recollection of the name corresponds to the actual object; therefore, this word "śyena" (hawk) applies to the brick-altar.
Consequently, when the altar is to be constructed using other materials, the word "śyena" is employed in a figurative sense.

For indeed, similarity between individuals cannot be established. Therefore, the connection observed is with the universal (*sāmānya*), not with the individual (*vyakti*). And it has been stated that words denote objects [as universals]. Consequently, the connection of the universal is not understood merely as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), but rather through its functional efficacy (*kāryataḥ*).

Furthermore, do even those things that are subordinate to a comparison possess the quality of being connected (anvayitva)? Certainly they do, in terms of cognition, but not in terms of action. Does something that is not connected to an action nonetheless possess the quality of being connected? It has been stated regarding the explanatory passages (arthavādas):

And regarding the mantra-words: why then is it not accepted that they refer to the generic form (*ākṛti*)? Because in the case of "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), they would not be subordinate (*anaṅgatva*) to the accomplishment of the ritual action.

But surely, if it were a mere secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), it would not be a constituent factor (*aṅga*); for a secondary indicator or a garment is not a factor in the comprehension of a specific distinction. Therefore, we do not know whether in some cases the individual instance (*vyakti*) is the recurring element (*anvayinī*) and in others the universal (*sāmānya*), nor where it is logical that "having become that" (*tadbhūtatva*) applies. Consequently, since the cause is not determined, once again—
Validity would thus follow. To this it is replied: the connection of the individual instance (*vyakti*) is not determined by way of its being that very thing (*tadbhūtatayā*).
For if the individual instance were the recurring element, then there would either be a recurrence of every individual instance, or else of a single individual instance.
Nor are both [the universal and the particular] perceived together; for everywhere, a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is observed that does not abandon the cognition of the universal.
But was it not said that there is a cognition of the universal by way of a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*)? That very point, however, is not understood.
For a so-called secondary characteristic does not indicate the object to be characterized by taking on its own form, as in the case of "where this crow is."
In the expression "Devadatta’s house," it is not understood that the house has the shape of a crow.
Furthermore, as for what was said— that for one who has seen a lion in its cage, the cognition of the lion arises from that very sight— [it is not so].
"The cage is understood; because of its power, the understanding of the form [of the lion] arises precisely from the understanding of the individual. This too is incorrect.

Why? Because people understand the cage as being of a different form from the form of the lion, whereas in the case of "Bring the cow," no other form is understood. Therefore, it is difficult to maintain that the individual is connected [to the word] while no other form is perceived.

To speak further: But surely, since the relation [of words to objects] is for the sake of a purposeful action (*kāryārtha*), and since that [action] is not possible through the mere form alone, the comprehension of the universal must necessarily be preceded by the manifestation [of the individual], in accordance with the cause [of cognition]. True, as it has been said [on p.

[The opponent says: "It possesses a father [i.e., it has a cause]. Even so, the comprehension of the concomitance (anvaya) extends only as far as the comprehension of the form (ākāra). Now, if the form is to be conceived as standing in the place of a cage, then there would be either a concomitance with mere individuals or a concomitance with a single individual. Let it be so; what harm is there to us? [The opponent replies: "The word would then be non-determinative (anadhyavasāyin). [The proponent asks: "Who said it is not? [The opponent replies: "Non-determinative..."
For how can it be said that the form lacks anvaya (inherence) with respect to the object to be accomplished (*vasāya*), as in the case of a horse when one says "bring the cow"? It is not, however,
like the case where the anvaya is not determined, such as clarified butter in the statement "the sugar-cubes are smeared."

Therefore, the position that [the word] indicates [the universal] is first of all incoherent. Now, it might be argued: the power of the word is innate, while its connection [to the object] is established through its effect (*kārya*). And this effect resides in the individual (*vyakti*); yet neither the mere individual nor a particular (*viśeṣa*) is apprehended. Rather, the substance is perceived as already connected with "cowness" (*gotva*). If that is so, then "cowness" has indeed been understood.

"Individuals are perceived as being connected"—do not say this. For positive concomitance (*anvaya*) culminates in an effect, and does not culminate in mere cognition. Just as in the command "Bring the man with the staff," it is not the bringing of the staff that is intended.
It is perceived and known; the same applies to the cow and other such things. You are ignorant of the distinction;
you have not grasped the distinction that has been stated. What was stated? This was stated:

where there is a distinction from another form, there another form serves as the indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). For example, in the case of "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*), it is precisely through the distinction from others who do not possess a staff that the specific individual possessing a staff is understood.

In the case of bringing [someone], there is no application of the word *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer). However, where it is understood simply as "one who possesses a staff" and not in a specific sense, there the application of such a [general] entity can indeed be asserted. But when a specific [individual] is understood, the word *daṇḍin*—

It does not reside in the staff. Or, if it is understood without distinction, does the word "staff-bearer" (daṇḍin) reside in the staff? True; it does not reside there by way of being the cause (nimitta). For in common usage, the status of being a cause is established only for that which is conjoined with another object. Furthermore, there is no comprehension of differentiation through the effect (kārya), as in the case of cows and so forth.

Furthermore, since no distinction among the causes is perceived, a distinction among the related entities as being the causes is not tenable; how much less so from the perspective of their effects? If there is no distinction based on the cause, then how is the specific nature understood in the case of "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*)? Is it not the case that the specific nature is understood from the effect? For the effect is indeed...

It culminates in the purpose, either in that which possesses the quality or in those things possessing it, such as the rice grains. But how are the rice grains understood to possess that quality? Through the context (*prakaraṇa*). Therefore, this comparison with the staff is not equivalent.

Therefore, since the universal is not present [in the individual], the [cognition] of the effect cannot find its final rest therein; nor can it be said that there is a lack of final rest when final rest is possible. But was it not stated that the lack of final rest arises because the object is the effect?
True, this was stated, provided that the effect is impossible [to be the object]. For the status of having the effect as its object occurs according to what is possible, not through modification.
It is precisely because of its activity, just as in the case of the instruments and so forth. But surely, even for those [instruments], there exists a modification (vikāra) in their own operation.
This is equally true for "cowness" (gotva) and the like; for that too is indeed active in the accomplishment of its operation.

Now, one might object: we do not perceive any modification in the universal (sāmānya) prior to its operation or subsequent to its completion, as we do in the case of instruments and the like. However, being subject to modification is not the cause for establishing an operation;

rather, it is the existence [of the operation] when that [modification] is present. Furthermore, the fulfillment of the meaning of an injunction does not occur in the absence of the cognition of the universal.

Thus it has been said: the manifestation of an object exactly as it is being perceived is established by the cognition of that which is being perceived. Therefore, the connection of the universal with its effect is logically consistent. However, its being denotable as something distinct [is not].

It is established by way of inclusion (*upādāna*). Therefore, the comprehension of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is preceded by the universal. However, with respect to the subject (*uddeśya*), there is the status of being a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇatva*) by virtue of its function, not by virtue of being non-identical with it. Thus, it is proven that [the word] functions through those elements which constitute the object as it is being understood, i.e., "those that have become such" (*tadbhūta*). And this has already been stated: that cognition from the word occurs in the form of a universal.

Here, the mention of "form" (*ākṛti*) is presented as an illustration; for even in the case of that which lacks form, there is no cognition of a qualified object without first grasping the qualifier. [Objection: "If it is then applied to another individual as well, then the individual is not the word-meaning.

What is the intended meaning? This is the intended meaning: for it is not possible to understand that a thing which has a known relation to one object can have a relation to another object without depending upon that first object. Nor is it possible [to know such a relation] for that which is unrelated.

The formal argument is as follows: If that which is relied upon is being employed, then there must be something distinct [from it]. For it has been demonstrated that the very nature of the individual (*vyakti*) is its uniqueness, since the individual is indeed devoid of all universals and particulars.

p. 162. “This is not a fault,” [it is argued], because this disjunction (*viyukti*) is common to all [individuals]. If that is the case, then it is disjunction that is expressed, not the individual (*vyakti*); thus, this results in nothing other than a universal (*sāmānya*). “No—” [the author replies].

"That object which is produced and which is the substratum of universals and particulars—that is the individual (vyakti). To whom is this answer given? It is given to one who attributes the nature of a universal to mere separation. But how can this be an answer to him? It is not.
A word grasps either a universal (*sāmānya*) or a particular (*viśeṣa*) as a mere indicator; it denotes only the substratum (*āśrayamātra*).
b176] But is not even the state of being a mere substratum a universal? No, it is said; for a universal is that which has a form—
The uniformity of those possessing internal distinctions is such that the so-called "substratum" (āśraya) possesses no distinct form apart from the "residents" (āśrayin).

Therefore, the intended meaning is that the application [of the word] is established because they are understood to be non-different. If this is the case regarding the application, then there is a contradiction; for the application of the word "cow" is never observed with respect to an individual horse, yet it would follow [that it should be].

In your own conceptualization, have you not yourself stated that there is non-perception? If that is so, then the observation of usage has not been relied upon. "Yes," it is said. How then, in the case of a cow born today, is the first—
Is the application [of the word] established? And yet it is observed [to occur]. Furthermore, the claim that "the application occurs only with respect to the individual" is a mere assertion;

for if the application were restricted solely to one individual, then linguistic usage would arise independently of other individuals, and consequently, a separate acquisition of meaning (vyutpatti) would be required for each subsequent individual. And if there is such a difference between them, this [would lead to an infinite regress].
It would have to be stated as "this is a cow" or "that is a cow," just as one says "this is an axle" or "that is an axle";
it could not, however, be based on a single derivation such as "this is a cow, and this too is a cow, and this too."

Therefore, the position that the individual is denoted is not tenable, because no other basis for linguistic usage (vyutpatti) is perceived. In that case, let both [the universal and the individual] be denoted; however, their status as subordinate or primary must be determined by their function (kārya). And thus, in the view where the primary is denoted—
It is doubted whether it is worldly (*laukika*) or Vedic (*vaidika*). Furthermore, in the case of the view that it is based on usage (*upādāna*), it remains simply a general rule (*sāmānyam*).
This is what was stated [by others]: "Both [types] belong to the venerable Pāṇini. Yet even this position is not tenable;
for being characterized by usage is a matter of effect (*kāryataḥ*), and not of cognition (*pratipattitaḥ*). And cognition is of the general...

[This is] the basis. Why? Because of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*). For even in the usage "he sprinkles the rice-grains" (*vrīhīn prokṣati*), which is directed toward individuals, the expression denotes [the object] precisely by way of its universal form.

If it is argued that [the substance] is determined through the individual instance (*vyakti*), we say no; for [the substance] is not cognized as being inherent in another individual instance. On the other hand, it has been stated that when a word is used with reference to the universal (*sāmānya*), the substance is determined precisely by way of a single form. This very point he expresses [in the verse]:
"due to a mental lapse."
Therefore, verbal cognition is not non-determinative; rather, it is indeed determinative because it arises from the cognition of a universal.
Thus ends the first chapter of the *Bṛhatī*.
The third quarter:
Bṛhatī [p. b180]
The Fourth Pāda of the First Adhyāya. It has been stated that the Vedic corpus exists for the sake of ritual action; therefore, everything else must be for that purpose. But this—
This is the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And he will state it in the second [book] and subsequent ones: "The definition of the means of valid cognition has been stated.

Why then is this introduced here? Is it that [the question] whether *udbhid* and so forth are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) or names of rituals (*karmanāmadheya*) is not appropriate as an introduction within the definition of the means of valid cognition? Certainly, for [that discussion] stands [in the second book].

The deliberation regarding the determination of a specific object is possible only if there is validity; however, if there is invalidity, since the object does not exist, what kind of deliberation on its specifics could there be? And as for that which was stated regarding the purposefulness of the sacred tradition (*samāmnāya*):

That which was explained as being possible because it is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*) is also untenable. For the impossibility of [the passage] being an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding the meaning of a mantra is not the reason for its being an injunction of an accessory. What then? The attainment of an action (*kriyāprāpti*) is the reason for its being an injunction of an accessory. And thus it has been stated by [the author] himself: "In a rite that has not been enjoined, an accessory..."

[The opponent argues: "The injunction would be purposeless. Furthermore, if the impossibility of being an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for a mantra were the reason for it being a subsidiary injunction (*guṇavidhi*), then the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*) would also be a subsidiary injunction.

As for what was also said—that the injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhāna*) will be meaningful in the *jyotiṣṭoma*, which is the archetype (*prakṛti*)—that too is incorrect, because even there the word expressing the quality is indeed heard, namely "by means of the *jyotiṣṭoma*. Now, if your intention is that in that case there will be an injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*), why does it not occur here as well? Or rather—

When one action is established, the other is merely an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhāna*) within that very same context; why then is it not the case here that, once [the primary action] is established, there is an injunction of its qualities?
Nor do we perceive any reason for such a restriction. Furthermore, there is the injunction of a qualified [action].

It is understood that [the action] arises as qualified. For it is not logical to enjoin another quality once a qualified action has already arisen, according to the principle: "And when there is a connection with something new, it is a quality, because the two sentences are equal."
Because of this designation, it is neither included within the definition [of the means of knowledge] nor is it a statement of the logical principle (*nyāya*). To this, it is replied:

This is indeed the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Now, it was argued that in the definition of the means of valid cognition, an inquiry into the determination of a specific object is not appropriate. This is not at all what has been presented here as the determination of a specific object. What then?
In this case, does it involve the injunction of an action (*karmavidhāna*), or is it merely the injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhāna*)? Since the injunction of an accessory is possible,
it is not logical to assume an injunction of an action, because the sentence is intent upon the accessory, as in the case of "the red cloth" (*raktapaṭavat*).

Therefore, because the prescription of an action is impossible, [the Veda] lacks authority. How so in the case of the view that it is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*)? Because it would have to rely upon a worldly action. For an injunction whose purpose is to enjoin a subordinate quality must necessarily rely upon a worldly action. What fault would there be if it relied upon a Vedic action? None at all. However, it is impossible for it to rely upon a Vedic one.

How is it impossible? Because [the word] "in all cases" (sarvatra) is heard as a qualifying term (*upapada*). Even so, why would there be a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*)? [The opponent replies: The activity toward the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) must be sought elsewhere. If it were from elsewhere, there would be the consequence of dependence (*sāpekṣatva*); and from dependence, a lack of authority follows. [The proponent replies: If, however, there is independence due to the prescription of a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*), as in the case of approaching a woman (*stryupagama*) and so forth, then how could there be a lack of authority?

Could it be so? This would indeed be the case if injunctions everywhere were solely for the sake of human ends (*puruṣārtha*). But what fault is there in a Vedic statement even when it has ritual action (*karman*) as its purpose? Indeed, none at all. However, there is simply an impossibility regarding the Vedic [statement].

How is it impossible? Because [the word] is heard everywhere as a subordinate term (*upapada*). Even so, why is there a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*)? The activity [of the word] must be sought elsewhere than in the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*); if it were from something else, there would be the consequence of dependence (*sāpekṣatva*). And from dependence, a lack of authority follows.
But if, as in the case of "acceptance" (*abhyupagama*) and so forth, independence is established through a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), how [is this so]?
Validity would [thus] result. This might be so if injunctions everywhere were solely for the sake of human goals;
however, some injunctions are perceived as being for the sake of ritual actions (*karma*). In that case, a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is not possible.
Furthermore, in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," what is being restricted? Is it not the agent (*kartṛ*), as in this [case of the] agent—?

The qualification does not hold, as has been demonstrated in the eleventh [chapter]. Furthermore, because the fruit is not something to be enjoined (*avidheya*), a restrictive rule (*niyama*) is impossible. If it is argued that "the action is restricted with regard to the fruit," it has already been stated that actions are not things to be enjoined, because sentences have other referents (*padārthāntara*). Therefore, another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) must be sought.

Or rather, it should be understood as a blind intuition (*andhapratibhā*). Why is there no injunction of an action possessing a quality, such as "bring the man with the staff" (*daṇḍinam ānaya*)? Because it is not understood. For in this case, the sense of possession (*matvartha*) is not conveyed by means of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth, as it is [ordinarily] represented; for that meaning belongs only to words ending in possessive suffixes (*matvantānām*).

If it is argued that [the object] is grasped through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), then it follows that there is dependence on something else. For secondary indication cannot be understood from the direct Vedic text (*śruti*). Therefore, it must be cognizable by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*).

As for what was stated—"It has been said that the Veda has this purpose; therefore, everything [in it] must be for that purpose"—this is not a reason for [accepting] a subordinate injunction (*guṇavidhi*). Indeed, it serves as a reason by way of refuting [the possibility of] a name (*nāmadheya*). But how, then, is the name refuted by this?
Because of the impossibility of its having that purpose. How [is there] "having that purpose" (*aidamarthya*)?

Is it not possible? It has been stated that the meaningfulness of injunctions, direct statements, mantras, and explanatory passages (arthavādas) arises from their being subject to a mandate (*niyoga*). However, this [meaningfulness] is not possible for a name because it is not something to be enjoined. Now, it might be argued: "The meaningfulness of those things which are not themselves enjoined was indeed stated to arise either through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) or through purposeful function; yet neither of these two is possible for this [name]. Therefore...

[It is] that which is to be enjoined. If it is that which is to be enjoined, then it is a quality (*guṇa*). Therefore, it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). But how [is this so] in the case of "one should sacrifice with *soma*"?

Is this an illustration of the injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*)? Or how could it not be possible? For even there, the sacrifice (*yāga*) is not enjoined. Let it be that the sacrifice is not enjoined; at least the accessory (*guṇa*) is being enjoined.
But surely even the injunction of an accessory is impossible, because [the term] is established as a name (*nāman*) in the usage of the elders.
For it is well-known that what is established is called "well-known" (*prasiddhi*). Now, one might argue that the practice of ritualists (*yājñika*) is also merely the practice of elders (*vṛddha*).

This is not so; because the practice of ritualists is preceded by worldly practice, and in the world, *udbhid* is not established as a name, since it is established as denoting a different thing (a sacrificial implement). Therefore, it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).
[Page b188] "Even so, the injunction of a quality in the archetype, the Jyotiṣṭoma, will be purposeful.
This commentary appears entirely improper. Why? Because even in the Jyotiṣṭoma, the word "Jyotiṣṭoma" [is present].
It is indeed injunctive. Even there, the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) must be sought. Who has said that it is not?
If this were so, an injunction would not be possible there, for the status of being a source for a subsidiary injunction (*guṇavidhi*) is indicated therein.
This is what is meant: by enjoining the subsidiary element in the statement "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), [the sacrifice] is already accepted—
From this, the accomplishment of the sacrifice follows. If it is accepted, then this [point] as well will be established therein.
Therefore, the word *jyotiṣṭoma* is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the accepted archetype (*prakṛti*), because a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhāna*) is impossible.

Thus it has been stated. Furthermore, in the view that it is a name (*nāmadheya*), the status of being a mandatory injunction (*niyoga*) is not possible, because the object to be enjoined is already conveyed by the root *yaj* (to sacrifice).

Moreover, a name assigned to that which is already enjoined does not assist the injunction; and its authority (*prāmāṇya*) consists precisely in its being subservient to the purpose of the injunction. Therefore, even in your own position, its authority must indeed be sought through another means of knowledge.
In our position, however, even the referent of the word is established through the linguistic usage of elders, or it may be a name.
To this, it is replied: "This sentence has a quality as its primary meaning."

What has been said is true; however, that [truth] applies to the *viniyoga* (the application of means). Furthermore, there is no need to look for a *viniyoga*. What then? There is a requirement for an *bhāva* (a being-to-be-accomplished), and this *bhāva* is expressed by "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*). Therefore, the *niyoga* (the mandate) has that as its object. And it is not thus...

The injunction has as its object a specific distinction that is established by another means of knowledge: namely, that "it is a different ritual action from the Jyotiṣṭoma. What is meant is this: it is established that the Vedic ritual action is distinct from the worldly one. And [the author] will demonstrate this in the sūtra: "From them, the action is to be understood."
Thus [it is asked]: "How then is there a repetition for the sake of a subordinate element (*guṇa*)?

That [repetition] intends the attainment of what is to be performed (*kartavyatā*), not the application (*viniyoga*). Or rather, is it not the case that the injunction (*niyoga*) follows the application? This, first of all, is the method of the author of the Sūtras regarding those whose meaning is the action (*bhāvārtha*).

[Page 191] For one who recites that "from those words, the action (kriyā) should be understood," is this sūtra—which stands as an opponent to the *niyoga*—to be taken according to its specific application (*viniyoga*)? Certainly. Otherwise, it would be like the maxim of the red cloth (*rakta-paṭa*).

The injunction of the hawk-sacrifice and others would follow; however, this has already been refuted on the grounds that it does not have a positive entity as its object. What, then, is the root of this methodological approach? We say it is "comprehension" (avagati).
But is comprehension not present even in the case of application (viniyoga)? Who said it was not? However, [in the case of injunction], it is the state of being something to be done (kartavyatā).

We have already stated that the object of existence (*bhāva*) is understood because existence has the nature of an action (*kārya*). Now, for what purpose is the understanding of application (*viniyoga*)? We reply: it is for the sake of the meaning of the action (*bhāvārtha*). How, then, is the subordination to a quality (*guṇa*) asserted?

When there is the attainment [of an object], it pertains to the state (*bhāva*). But surely, when a subordinate word (*upapada*) is heard, the state alone is not understood as having the status of an object, as in the case of "the cloth becomes red. It has already been demonstrated that it is not merely the becoming of the cloth that is determined. And by whom was it said that the state is "alone"?

It becomes the object; however, it has been stated that this object belongs to the injunction (*niyoga*). Nor does it obstruct its connection with other words, for it is understood as being precisely qualified, like a "red cloth" (*raktapaṭa*). But how—[p.

Qualities such as *rudrabhida* (the "splitter of Rudra") exist and then attain the status of qualifiers. Is the relationship between qualifier and qualified established solely by way of being a quality? No, for it is also seen in the case of names: "This Brāhmaṇa is Ḍittha," or "This Kṣatriya is Ḍabittha.
But how, in this case, is there the status of a name? Because it is understood through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). But how [is that understood]?

How is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) determined? From the use of the instrumental case. For the meaning of the instrumental case exists in the sacrifice; it is stated that this [meaning] is established for it by this [word]. And the instrumental case is heard in words such as *udbhid*.
Therefore, it is understood that "by means of the *udbhid* sacrifice."
This is incorrect—for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not based on having the same case ending;
what then? It is based on the cognition of a single referent. If it were based on having the same case ending...

If [the word *aruṇayā* were taken as an adjective], then in the expression *aruṇayā ekahāyanyā*, there would be no connection between the substance (*dravya*) and the quality (*guṇa*) with the action; rather, there would be only a mutual relationship between them, like "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*). For this very reason, even though they share the same case-ending, the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "white," "horse," "man," and "elephant" is not perceived. And because of their having a single referent, this [word] refers to Devadatta.
Thus it is understood. Therefore, the case-ending is not the cause of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

To this it is replied: It has been stated that because the meaning consists of an action (*bhāvārtha*), the obligation to perform the act pertains to the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice), and not to the meaning of the nominal stem (*nāman*). Furthermore, a relationship is indeed perceived. If that [relationship] were accepted as being caused by a quality (*guṇa*), then—

The elision of the *matup* suffix must be assumed. However, if it is a name (*nāmadheya*), then the relationship is based on another word that is not so assumed. And this is appropriate for the case of "samāna-" [in *samānajātīya*].
Because of the connection with the case-ending. As for what was shown regarding "aruṇayā" (with the red one), there the relation to the action belongs to both [the substance and the quality].

But here, since no other object is heard, whose related thing does the third case express? It expresses nothing other than that which denotes the action. Therefore, this third case has as its sole fruit the mere indication [of the relationship]. Now, if it is merely an indication...

The nominative case must be employed. That [rule] teaches non-distinction from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), not non-distinction from the meaning of the word (*pada*). Thus it has been illustrated by the example: "The Brahmin named Ḍittha ate.
But surely, since there is no comprehension of a single unified meaning, what will the case-ending accomplish?

In this case, it is better to assume simply the elision of the *matup* suffix. Alternatively, both [the noun and the verb] may have the sense of an injunction (*niyoga*). First of all, it has been stated that both do not have the sense of an injunction, because an injunction has as its object that which is to be accomplished (*kārya*). Furthermore, it has been stated that a noun does not denote that which is to be accomplished.
Granted that a name may denote an effect through its connection with its constituent parts—this is true, provided the view is that [the name] is not distinct [from its parts].
