But when there is a relation by virtue of being a separate category (*padārthāntara*), who can deny that it has an established meaning (*siddhārtha*)? And it has already been stated that what has an established meaning is not the object of an injunction (*aniyogaviṣaya*). Therefore, because it conforms to the connection with its constituent parts, it is established that its meaning is not distinct [from those parts].
And because it is non-different from the name, the lack of contact with an injunction is avoided.
But surely, as much as is said by "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), so much would also be "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*."
This defect would arise if the means of valid cognition were to conform to the purpose; however, it is the purpose that conforms to the means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, it is observed that names serve as auxiliaries to the meaning of other sentences. Therefore, it is established that the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is independent.
"In which case there is an instruction regarding a quality (*guṇa*), there is a primary connection [of that quality with the action].
It was stated that even the name will be purposeful through its connection with a quality and a result (*phala*). To one who considers that to be incorrect, the subject matter—
In certain specific cases, an illogicality is demonstrated. As for how it is illogical, it is stated as follows: first, for the purpose of connecting the qualities (*guṇa*), there are five—
"Ten other [terms] are names," such as "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā," which serves to connect them with a specific result.

In this regard, the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is as follows: it is indeed appropriate that terms such as "udbhidā yajeta" (one should sacrifice with the udbhid) are names, because they stand in grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the root *yaj* (to sacrifice). The same applies to terms such as "ājya" and so forth.

In the case of "They praise with the *ājya*s," there is a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the act of praising; however, where such coreferentiality with the meaning of the verbal action is not perceived— as in "The *ājya* hymns are fifteen"— there is no comprehension of a name [of a rite].
Even if the meaning were inclusive, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would not be perceived—as in the case of "the fifteen *ājya* [chants]";

there, no understanding of it as a name exists. Although it was stated that being a name follows from coreferentiality even when the meaning is inclusive, that is not present here. Therefore, it cannot be asserted that the name has a purposeful function through its connection with a quality (*guṇopabandha*).

It is indeed appropriate [to grant] meaningfulness when there is a connection with a quality (*guṇa*). However, regarding the connection with a fruit (*phala*), since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible, why would there not be meaningfulness in the case of "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *citriṇī* [offering]"? It is replied: there is no meaningfulness, because the injunction "one desiring cattle should sacrifice" is already established. For in that case...
The specific sacrifice is obtained from its very proximity, not from its name. Let it be that there is no specific [sacrifice];
however, its status as a name cannot yet be refuted. And who has said that its status as a name is being refuted? There is simply no purpose [in doing so].
Thus much is the objection. But how, then, can there be an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhāna) in the case of "one desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Citrā"?

Such is the injunction of a quality: here, a specific sacrifice already known is enjoined for the sake of a fruit; for when the specific [sacrifice] is already known, the cognition provided by another word does not serve to establish that specific [sacrifice]. Why? Precisely because it is already known. Where...
For an object that is to be enjoined must be understood solely through the words connected within its own sentence; the specific qualification thereof is understood from those very words.
However, an object already known from another sentence does not require connection with words in its own sentence for the sake of its own comprehension.

Grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that which is not intended [as the primary object] is non-verbal. Therefore, the word *citrā* must be understood as that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*). In cases where the specific distinction is understood from the accompanying word (*upapada*) alone—since that which has been enjoined is not the subject under discussion (*aprakṛta*)—let there be a purpose [for the injunction] there. However, in this case, it has been demonstrated that such a purpose does not exist at all. This remains true even when [the action] is not the subject under discussion.

Nor does it assist by way of being a name (*nāmadheya*). For if [the context] were not already established, it would simply be another ritual action (*karmāntara*). And in that case, the injunction of the meanings of both words has been demonstrated, as in "He performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice" within the *Kuṇḍapāyinām ayana*. Therefore, there is no connection with a fruit for either an action already produced or one currently being produced.

Nor is there meaningfulness [in the other case]. Therefore, where the word *citrayā* is applicable, an injunction must be inferred there—for instance, in the passage "one desiring cattle should sacrifice"—because that [word] does not require [the inference of another injunction]. Consequently, by means of the connection between the quality (*guṇa*) and the fruit (*phala*), the purpose—
This is incorrect.

To this it is replied: this is not incorrect; for where another quality (*guṇa*) is enjoined, there the very name of the previously established action is understood. Indeed, a quality cannot be enjoined with respect to that which is not an action, since it must depend [upon an action].

Because of the statement of the principle that "the application [of a word] follows from its true nature," and because their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) establishes that it is a name, it is indeed capable of denoting the named object. Therefore, it is logical that it is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) through its connection with a quality.

This is appropriate in the case of *ājya* and so forth; but how is it so in the case of *citrayā*? For in that instance, the specific [meaning] is understood precisely because of the context (*prakṛtatva*).

It cannot be said that the suffix has a meaningful purpose. Certainly, it can be so even there, provided that [the action] does not already exist; for if it were already produced, an injunction regarding its fruit would be untenable due to the contradiction with the mention of a quality; this [injunction] is for the sake of the fruit.

It is not for the sake of a quality (*guṇa*), because no specific [quality] is understood; and when nothing is understood, there is no determination (*anadhyavasāya*); and from the absence of determination follows invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*). Therefore, it is rightly said that [the name] is purposeful by being connected with a result (*phala*) through its status as a designation (*nāmatayā*). Furthermore, these [names] are not etymological (*yaugika*).

Where, then, is the refutation of its being based on etymological derivation (yaugikatva) applicable? This is the intended meaning: for if it were based on etymological derivation, there would be the establishment of denoting the sacrifice under discussion;
just as in the case of "Give wages to the cook," [the relationship holds] even in the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
The establishment of the designation "cook" as intended in the context follows from this; therefore, it has been stated that these [words] are not etymological (*yaugika*).

However, when there is the denotation of a genus (*jāti*), here [the word] possesses the status of being the predicate (*vidheya*) itself. For the denotation of an individual (*vyakti*) indeed [serves as] a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

It is dependent [on other factors], and it does not denote the individual (vyakti) through an improper derivation. Thus, because "citrayā" denotes merely a quality (guṇa), it is equivalent to those [words] that denote a genus (jāti). Furthermore, in the statement "one should sacrifice with the citrā," it is a reference (anuvāda) to a sacrifice because [the sacrifice] is already known; it is not an injunction (vidhi) for a sacrifice.
What is demonstrated by this? It is that the word *citrayā* lacks expectancy (*anākāṅkṣitatva*).
When there is a lack of expectancy, there is an absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); due to that absence, it is not a name (*nāmadheya*).
Therefore, in the injunction of a result (*phalavidhi*), it is understood that it does not function as a name. [This is so] when one assumes a quality (*guṇa*) and a result (*phala*).

What is intended by the objection that "the root *yajati* [the act of sacrificing] is not intended to be expressed"? For even in the case of a connection between a quality (*guṇa*) and a fruit (*phala*), the name itself would have no meaningful purpose. On the contrary, this very point must be refuted by the proponent of the final view (*rāddhāntin*), who asserts that the name does indeed possess meaning.
Therefore, this fragment of the Bhāṣya that revolves in the mind is indeed entirely irrelevant. To this it is replied:
205] It is certainly not possible to prevent the postulation of a result for a subordinate element (guṇa). Why?
Because the root *yajati* (to sacrifice) is not intended [as the primary object]; and when it is not intended as such, a subordinate factor (*guṇa*) cannot be enjoined for the sake of a result.
For the cause of the connection between a ritual action and its result is the performance of that action from elsewhere.
And there is no impeller of the meaning of the root *yaj* other than the injunction for one desiring cattle. Therefore...

If the connection with the desire for cattle is not abandoned, then the term *citrayā* remains merely a name. Therefore, since there is no mutual expectancy between the two, one must understand that in some cases there is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) corresponding to a quality.
Even if one assumes the injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), there is no recourse to metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

For it has been stated that when resorting to metaphorical indication, there is the fault of [the word] having another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) as its object of cognition; and this same fault applies here as well due to the relationship with the coreferential term (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

Since the entity does not exist [as a primary injunction], it is established that this is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). Therefore, it is established that the name is purposeful by virtue of its connection with a quality and a result. It is replied: An injunction of a quality is not possible here; for when there is an injunction of the meaning of a name, the established entity is enjoined as entering into the ritual action, but not the object itself as something to be performed.

What follows from this? This results: where this quality, being established, serves as a means for the ritual action, there it must be enjoined. Therefore, its injunction pertains to the animal (*paśu*);
and when it is enjoined therein, another quality of it—namely, femaleness (*strītva*)—must also be enjoined. If, however, [it were otherwise]...

In that case, regarding the procedure for the Sārasvatī sacrifice, the connection with the desire for cattle (paśukāma), which is understood there, would have to be abandoned; furthermore, the attainment of the qualities of the Agniṣomīya [sacrifice] would be sublated in the Sārasvatī.

Therefore, since this [injunction] is set aside by its own syntactical connection within the *agnīṣomīya* sacrifice—which serves as the archetype (*prakṛti*) for all sacrifices involving living beings as the sacrificial substance—therein two things remain unestablished and must be enjoined anew. Consequently, it is impossible for this to be an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*). Thus, its status is that of being the cause for the perceived syntactical connection.

It is logical to assume [the status of] a name (*nāmadheya*). And it has already been stated that such [a quality] is not possible here in the case of a name. Therefore, its status as a name is established. Furthermore, it has also been demonstrated that it is purposeful by way of its connection with a result. Likewise, in the case of the injunction "The *ājya* hymns are fifteen," if it were a prescription of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), there would be the prescription of two qualities; and that is not possible.

Therefore, it should be understood as a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) in this single instance. And that characteristic belongs to the word *ājya* itself, which denotes an action already known from another scriptural passage (*vākya*). Thus, through a traditional succession—

The understanding of the relationship [between the word and its meaning] is not abandoned. As for the statement, "There are fifteen *ājya* [chants]," even that which was said—that there is no indication (*lakṣaṇā*) here in the view that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*)—is also incorrect. Why? Because wherever the *ājyas* are enjoined by the words "the *ājyas* come to be" (*ājyāni bhavanti*), that [sentence] must be expressed with the verb *bhavati*. Therefore, in this case...
The statement that "they possess clarified butter" (*ājyavanti*) is itself a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
As for the claim that the status of being a name for the ritual action (*karman-nāmadheya*) is unestablished, that is established because it serves as a figurative indication of the action;
furthermore, since the ground for application (*pravṛtti-nimitta*) exists everywhere—as in the case of [the phrase] "those who went toward the race" (*yad ājim īyuḥ*).
Thus,
etc. Now, why are the *ājya* verses not enjoined in the *stotras* as qualified by the number fifteen?

Thus, what has been set forth here that was not already refuted? The meaning of the two words is prescribed elsewhere. What would happen in this case? The intention is that there would be no repetition of the sentence. This would indeed be established if the connection between these two were already established prior to the prescription, as in the case of "to Agni Pāvaka."

But that [injunction] does not exist; therefore, the connection between these two is based solely on the subject matter of the injunction. Consequently, it is impossible for the meanings of both words to be the objects of the injunction.

Now, why is it that an injunction [of a relationship] is not possible even between two things that lack a connection, such as fire and Prajāpati? Because a mutual connection must be understood; and since no such connection established by another means of knowledge exists, it must be accepted as being based solely on the injunctive statement itself. Therefore, this point is also established.
"This is also its name," and there is another treatise that makes this known.

But by what specific distinction is there a suspicion here that this is an injunction of a subordinate element (*guṇavidhi*), given that there is no need for the indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*)? For even as an injunction of a subordinate element, the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible. Thus it has been shown: "The *hotra* (oblation) is for Agni in this"—this is a compound expressing the oblation, where the sense of the subordinate member [is coreferential].
Even by way of a formal injunction, it remains a prescription of a quality (guṇavidhi), as in the case of "the priests wear golden garlands.
This is certainly appropriate in the case of "he offers the Agnihotra," but as for "he pours the Āghāra libation" [p.

How so? There is no purpose here for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); rather, since the status of [the word] as denoting an action (*karmavacanatā*) is not perceived here, it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). This pouring (*āghāraṇa*) is enjoined only where there is a substance to be poured. But is it not the case that the sacrifice, having a substance to be poured, already possesses the act of pouring by virtue of being accomplished through the *āhavanīya* fire?
What is the purpose of the injunction for the *āghāra*? The intention is that this subsequent *āghāra*, following the *homa* and the first *āghāra*, is for the sake of purifying the substance.

This is the view of one who considers the word *āghāra* to be a term denoting an action (*karmasādhana*). For this very reason, it has been shown that [the *āghāra*] is like the *upāṃśuyāja*. Therefore, in this example, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is based solely on the fact that [the term *āghāra*] does not denote an action.

It has been stated that even though the Agnihotra is an injunction regarding a ritual action, an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi) is not contradictory therein. To this, it is replied: an injunction of a subordinate quality is not possible here. Why? Because [the quality] is already established.

Regarding the qualities: those qualities which are presented as being subject to injunction are already obtained from elsewhere. First, the fire [is obtained] from the passage "to Agni and to Prajāpati. The pouring of the oblation is also [obtained from] "he pours the oblation continuously" and "he pours the oblation straight."
From such passages as these:
214] Why is this said to be incoherent? What is so incoherent about it? It has been stated that in the *darvihoma* there is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*).

Furthermore, this injunction—"to Agni and to Prajāpati"—does not apply solely to the *darvihoma*. Likewise, it has been stated that the pouring of the *āghāra* libation pertains to the *upāṃśuyāja*. Nor do the qualities such as continuity (*santata*) and so forth apply to the *upāṃśu*...

It appears that these are injunctions of accessory details (*guṇavidhi*) for the *upāṃśuyāja*, like the term "sky" (*viyat*). To this we reply: If it were the case of an injunction of an accessory detail, this injunction would apply only to the *darvihoma* and would already be included within the *upāṃśuyāja*.

In that case, the principle of "being known from another source" (*tatprakhyatā*) would not be the reason for the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*). [Objection: Certainly, it is the reason for the final conclusion.

How so? For even that designation based on similarity applies only to the *darvihoma*, because it depends upon another context, just as in the case of "he performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice. Likewise, the expression "he pours the *āghāra* continuously" refers only to the *upāṃśuyāja*.

Because they depend on a substance that serves a purpose, just as in the case of the injunction "he pours the *āghāra* libation. Furthermore, the status of being a name (*nāmatā*) belongs to those very [acts] and to the *upāṃśuyāja*. The "beloved of the gods" (the opponent) is ignorant of what is not already established elsewhere, since the prescription of the qualities is accomplished from another source, and because a name is not itself something to be prescribed; rather, it is the meaning of the verbal suffix in "he offers the *agnihotra*" that is being prescribed.

What else can be understood from this statement other than that, once the meaning of the verbal root has been enjoined, the phrases "to Agni" and "to Prajāpati" refer specifically to that [root-meaning] due to the context? Therefore, it is established that this is indeed its name. Similarly, in the case of "he pours the libation" (*āghārayati*), once the injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhāna*) has been precluded, what else remains to be enjoined apart from the meaning of the verbal root? And that—

[217] Because of the connection between the substance and the deity, the *yajati* (sacrificial act) is like the *harati* (offering); therefore, acts such as *santata* (continuous) and so forth are likewise that very same act.
Consequently, it is established that this too is merely a name for that [act]; the meaning is that one performs the *āghāra* (libation) continuously. How so?
Furthermore, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) here, because in the phrase "to Agni and to Prajāpati," multiple attributes are being enjoined.

A syntactical split—defined as the enjoining of multiple attributes—does not occur when multiple qualifiers of a single *kāraka* (grammatical participant) are enjoined. For what is called "multiple attributeness" refers to the enjoining of other related entities (*saṃbandhin*), not the enjoining of other substances (*dravya*).
And there is also designation by that [name].
Here, conventional terms (*rūḍhiśabda*) serve as examples, such as *śyena*, *ājya*, *pṛṣṭha*, and so forth.
But what, then, is the distinction here from the discussion regarding the word *udbhid*? This is it:
etymological application (*yoga*) conforms to the basis for its usage (*pravṛttinimitta*), whereas conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) does not follow etymological application. But surely [p.
Even on the view that it is a name (*nāmadheya*), one need not assume that the term *śyena* follows from its etymological derivation (*yogānuvartitva*). What then?

It is a figurative designation (*gauṇam abhidhānam*). A conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) does not preclude figurative usage, because figurative designation is rooted in convention. Therefore, since the elision of the possessive suffix (*matub-lopa*) lacks any basis of proof, it is better to resort to figurative usage alone.
It is precisely to remove this very misconception that the Blessed Commentator has cited this example.

It is appropriate to say that in cases such as *udbhid* and others, the term is a name (*nāmadheya*) because of the fear of dropping the suffix *-matup* and because of the recourse to etymological derivation (*yoga*); but it is not so in the following case— [p.

In the case of the *śyena* sacrifice, one resorts to another elision out of fear of [further] elision; for the application of secondary (gauna) meanings occurs when the suffix *vat* has been elided. Therefore, it was argued again by the prima facie (pūrvapakṣin) position that it is better to simply resort to the elision of the *matup* suffix, because this preserves the connection with the directly stated (śrauta) meaning.
To this, it is replied: even if it were a conventional term (*rūḍhi*), it is more logical that it be a name (*nāmadheya*). But is it not so? [The opponent asks: No.
It has been stated that conventional usage (rūḍhi) follows etymological derivation (yoga). However, even etymological derivation does not necessarily follow conventional usage. [Objection:

But surely, in this case, the previously perceived conventional usage sets aside the etymological derivation. [Reply: True, provided that the meaning of the sentence is preceded by the comprehension of the cause (nimitta). thus, it is demonstrated in the remainder of the passage that conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is not accepted, as in the phrase "when [he] won the race" (*yadājimī-*).

In cases such as "yūpa" (sacrificial post) and so forth, this is appropriate for substances like clarified butter (*ājya*); but how is it so in the case of the *śyena* sacrifice? It is due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
For coreferentiality remains uncontradicted even in figurative denotation, since the meaning of the suffix *-vat* is what is to be enjoined.

Furthermore, if there were an elision of the *matup* suffix, a difference of substratum (*bhinnādhikaraṇatā*) would be unavoidable, because the meaning of the possessive suffix (*matvartha*) would then be the thing to be enjoined. Therefore, since it is established that the suffix is elided and not the *matup*, its status as a name (*nāmadheya*) is proven.
[This is stated in the sūtra: "In the case of a name, because of the mention of a quality (*guṇaśruteḥ*)."

This section is intended to imply all such [names].

Because of the presentation of the term *tantra* as the designation for the root *yaj* (to sacrifice). Therefore, this [is stated] for the purpose of refuting the designation of a *tantra*.
The present section is commenced. [Objection:

If that is so, then *udbhid* and others should also be cited as examples here; certainly they should. [Question: Why, then, was "one desiring sovereignty should sacrifice with the *vājapeya*" cited? [Answer: This is a challenge regarding the *śiṃśipā* tree.

"Because the two actions are equal," it is said. This observation pertains to the Vājapeya sacrifice, yet it applies to all cases as well. Therefore, it is stated that the position of a quality-injunction (*guṇavidhi*) is superior. Why? Because in this way, the referent of the word—such as *udbhid* and so forth—becomes something connected to a specific action (*kārya*). On the other hand, under the position of a name (*nāmadheya*), the referent of the word would be merely the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*).

Since that which is enjoined does not possess the nature of being an *udbhid* (a sacrificial implement), and there is no injunction for the *udbhid* itself, the mention of a cause would be for the purpose of non-engagement,

But was it not said that one must resort to a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), which is not the literal meaning of the word? It is replied: that very [indication] does not exist. How so? For the meaning of the verb (*ākhyātārtha*) is understood as being of a single form even in the relationship between cause and effect.
Indeed, it is only while being brought about (*sādhyamāna*) that it is the means (*sādhana*). When both are thus understood, why [resort to indication]?

This involves a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*). Therefore, this meaning is established: "by means of the *vājapeya* sacrifice one performs a sacrifice, and by means of that sacrifice one attains sovereignty" (*svārājya*). This is a different expression based on observation; it is not, however, a different understanding of the word-meanings themselves.

Is it not the case that this is a property of the object (*vastu*) and not a property of the word (*śabda*), for the word conveys one thing as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*) and another as something to be referred to (*uddeśya*)? True. However, because it possesses both forms, it is thus denotable; and even when denoting both, the word *yajeta* is capable of presenting the two related entities. If it is indeed capable—

"The injunction of qualities and the validity [of the Veda] are established. Not so; those two are incapable, for if they lack capacity, what will the capacity of the denotation accomplish? Therefore, because both meanings are enjoined, there is an [injunction] of the action—

Moreover, the possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) is contradictory. Therefore, by the arguments stated above, the position that [the word] is a name (*nāmadheya*) alone is consistent. But its qualities should be enjoined. Why is this section commenced? What is the point of this question?

The *kapāla* would not be the subject [of the injunction]. If the *aṣṭākapāla* were the subject, what follows from that? This follows:
the state of being an *aṣṭākapāla* would have to be understood as unenjoined. And that which is unenjoined—*aṣṭāka-* [is not established].
There is a protector.

Is it not the case that what is cooked on eight potsherds is "eight-potsherded" (aṣṭākapāla) in the worldly sense; or is it based on scriptural injunction, because of the statement "he cooks on potsherds"? It cannot, for now, be based on scriptural injunction.
It is possible [that the number eight is intended], because the number eight is heard [in the text]. If it is argued that "the number is being enjoined," we say no;
for that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), such that there would be an *āgneya* [cake] when there is a number, and a number when there is an *āgneya*.

Therefore, an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi) is not possible, nor has it been stated that it is a name (nāman). How then was it stated by the author of the Bhāṣya that it is a name? Where was it stated? It was stated in the introduction: "Is this a name or an injunction of a quality? And by refuting the injunction of a quality, it follows that it is a name.
What has been said is true, but not with respect to that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*). Therefore, by the mention of the name, its well-known meaning (*prasiddhārthatā*) is demonstrated.
And since such renown does not occur without another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), the dependence of the application (*prayoga*) is shown.
To this it is replied: this would indeed be so, if, in the connection with number and the connection with the deity, there were no mutual...

There would have to be a basis; however, that does not exist. [The basis is] the injunction of the deity for the eight-pot-sherd offering (*aṣṭākapāla*). But was it not said that this [deity] is unestablished?
Is it unestablished even as a denotation? No, it is unestablished as an effect (*kāryatayā*). This is indeed accepted.

For this very reason, it is enjoined. Therefore, the non-establishment of the expression [of the object] subverts the injunction; however, there is no non-establishment even as a thing to be accomplished (*kāryatayā*). Consequently, the injunction of the object "eight-potherd" (*aṣṭākapāla*) is established just like the object of the root *yaj* (sacrifice). And this well-known expression has been demonstrated by the author of the Bhāṣya.

"One does not accept what has been cooked by another. Therefore, just as the meaning of the *yaj* [root] is well-established, so too is the meaning of this *taddhita* suffix; hence, there is no contingency of being dependent on something else. Nor is it possible for the meaning to be already established [by another means], as is the case with the *agnihotra*.
Regarding the lack of refinement of the *barhis* grass and the clarified butter (*ājya*):

this section is incidental. But what is the connection? It is observed that even with a meaning that is to be enjoined, there is a syntactical connection with the meaning of a noun; and this word *ājya* is also such [a term].

In this world, [the term] is seen to be based solely on its ritual function (*karmanimitta*). Therefore, this [term] *ājya* as well should be applied to the clarified butter by virtue of its connection with the ritual action (*kāryānvayin*).
But surely, it is sometimes seen even when not based on a ritual function, as in "clarified butter is for sale" (*ājyaṃ krayyam*) or "having taken the sacrificial grass" (*barhirādāya*).

"The cows have gone. For a usage that is universally recognized ought to be considered Vedic (śrauta), not one originating from a single region. Why? Because it is only when a word is already well-established in its primary Vedic sense that a secondary (gauṇa) application is possible.

Furthermore, this [word "ghṛta"] is not well-known in all cases as having the sense of clarified butter (*ghṛta*). For that which is not well-known, a figurative application (*gauṇatva*) regarding clarified butter is not tenable. However, where it is employed in a partial sense while accomplishing an action, its figurative application regarding clarified butter is established because of its usage based on the action. Therefore, it is logical that it functions solely for the sake of the ritual purpose (*kāryārthatā*).
To this it is replied: the connection [of the grass] as being for the sake of the effect is not tenable, because it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*):

namely, that there is sprinkling of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and, conversely, the sacrificial grass [is defined] by the sprinkling. How then is it not so in the case of the eight-pot-sherd cake (*aṣṭākapāla*)?

Is it not said that [the name] is established through direct designation (*abhidhāna*)? But here, the designation is based solely on the function (*kārya*); thus there is a difference. How is it so in the case of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*)? Since there is no establishment from any other source, this is a recourse when there is no other way (*agatikā gatiḥ*). What is this "recourse when there is no other way"? Is it not understood from the scripture (*śāstra*)? [We reply: Only if such a well-known usage (*prasiddhi*) exists.
Is it not understood? However, when a word’s meaning is not well-known, because the purpose of the injunction remains unobstructed, it is postulated.
As for what was said—that a secondary (gauṇa) sense cannot apply to a universal ruler (sārvabhauma) because the primary (śrauta) sense is not established—[that is incorrect], for...

"But it is possible for [the word] to be used in its primary sense when residing in its proper location. It is not necessarily the case that worldly people employ a secondary (gauṇa) usage solely for the sake of establishing a well-known meaning, as they do with the word "king" even when applied to a Kṣatriya. In that case too, the same fault applies, for people employ a secondary usage for the purpose of conveying a similarity. Thus, they employ a secondary usage even without the cognition of that [primary object].
This is a forced argument. To this it is replied: the relationship between a word and its meaning does not depend upon the speaker’s intention;
for it is the relationship itself that necessitates the intention.
For it has been stated regarding the *Gopotalikā* and other such works that, because they do not understand the incapacity [of the speaker], people employ them as if they were beginningless.
In the same way, here too, due to a lack of understanding of the intention (*vivakṣā*), some speakers employ [a word] devoid of intention toward a different meaning.
How, then, is this understood? From the observation of usage in both the world and the Veda. In the Veda...

Having thus established that *ājya* is the subject, he praises it using the word "ghee" (*ghṛta*). Even in common worldly usage, one finds the expression "ghee is for sale," which is employed independently of any specific action it might accomplish. Now, one might argue that even in that case, it could be said that the intended meaning is not understood.

The resolution regarding the *vaitasa* and other such cases has already been stated; it is that when there is a conflict, a determination is reached through similarity to Vedic usage. But what is the purpose of this incidental discussion? It is simply the absence of a definitive conclusion.
Yet, the author of the *Bhāṣya* has demonstrated the distinction specifically regarding ritual action (*karman*); therefore, indeed, there is no definitive conclusion.
The purpose: Since the determination [of the meaning] is established through resolution, the purpose remains indeed [the same].
This is because of the connection with the purpose in the case of the *prokṣaṇī* waters.

For what purpose is this a separate topic? An exception to the rules of usage based on traditional authority (*smṛti*) regarding those originating from the whole earth and from a single region is being stated. But how can an exception to usage be stated on the basis of traditional authority? It is because usage is possible in accordance with traditional authority. For:

The connection of the suffix *a* with two [words] is possible, as in "he brings the sprinkling waters" (*prokṣaṇīr āsādayati*) and "we are troubled by the sprinkling waters" (*prokṣaṇībhir udvejitāḥ smaḥ*). Therefore, the determination is based on traditional usage (*smṛti*). The rest has been explained.
The same applies to the case of the fire produced by friction (*nirmanthya*).

What is the excess here? This is the excess: the traditional authority (*smṛti*) is also over-extensive, because [the fire] is seen even when the friction has not been performed for long. Therefore, there is no definitive conclusion even from the *smṛti*.
Thus he thinks: since the Smṛti prescribes without qualification, its specific application cannot be set aside.
If it is argued that it sets aside the knowledge of non-specificity, we say no; for it does not set it aside, because the specific application is fully established.
[This refers] to the specific case of *ravi*. Therefore, this is also like the previous [case]. For that reason, it was stated, "it is thus.
If it is argued that there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the *vaiśvadeva* [offering], how then can it be an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*)?

Is there doubt here regarding its being a name? In this case, the view that it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) is more appropriately consistent with grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), because the action (*bhāva*) is the meaning of the suffix. Why, then, is it not a name?
Why is it introduced by that [word]? Because there is no basis for an injunction due to the absence of a subject matter. Why is there an absence of a subject matter?

Because the rites under discussion are already occupied by Agni and others through direct scriptural statement (śruti). Why does this not constitute a different rite? That too is not determined, because the *āmikṣā* is the subject matter under discussion.

Therefore, if you think that independence cannot be understood either by name or by quality— that it is impossible to determine independence— then let it be so; [let there be] the injunction of qualities.
The determination [of the meaning] occurs through the understanding of the relationship between the meanings of nouns and verbs. But was it not said that there is an absence of an object?

That was indeed poorly stated. How is it poorly stated? For the postulation of an action (*kārya*) arises from what is heard (*śruta*), not from the action itself. What does this mean? This is as follows: the obstruction by a quality (*guṇa*) enjoined at the time of origin (*utpattiśiṣṭa*) is the cause for the lack of understanding [of another].
But it does not apply when there is a contradiction with what has already been understood. Furthermore, this term *vaiśvadeva* refers precisely to the meaning of the verb;
it cannot exclude Agni and the others—who are related to that verbal meaning—from being denoted by the word *vaiśvadeva*.
The [words] are capable [of denoting the agent]; they preclude the status of being the object of another related entity, but they do not preclude the status of being the denoted meaning itself.

What follows from this? From this it follows that, for the sake of establishing the denoted meaning, there is the acquisition of another related entity; however, fire and the others, who are related by way of origination (*utpatti-sambandhin*), do not obstruct [this]. Likewise, the fruit-cup (*phalacamasa*) is implied as something to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*).

Soma possesses the status of being a means for the sacrifice; therefore, there is a determination [of its use] through option (*vikalpa*), and not on account of the context (*prakaraṇa*) nor because of a direct injunction (*pratyakṣavidhāna*). For the context does not pertain to the substance.
If this is so, let it be merely a name; for the connection with another quality is only for the sake of making the designation possible.
It is conceptualized; however, for those remaining who possess incomparable authority, there is no conceptualization, and that is established as being merely a designation.

But surely, if the meaning of the individual parts were understood, it would not be connected to the action (kārya). It is not logical for that which is already connected to be further connected; yet the meaning [of the word *vājina*] is already connected with the curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*). Therefore, the lack of connection to the action does not suffice to prevent its denotation. Consequently, neither an option (*vikalpa*) nor a repetition (*āvṛtti*) can be postulated.
Therefore, it is logical that the determination of the action is made solely on the basis of its name.

But how can there be the designation "vaiśvadeva" for what is not dedicated to the Viśvedevas? It is because of the restatement [of the action] when a secondary injunction (guṇavidhi) is being formulated.

It is established. This is true only if it is established by way of a mandatory injunction (*vidhāna*). For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that *āmikṣā* is not denoted [by the word]. And the status of being the subject under discussion (*prakṛtatva*) is equal for both. Which, then, of these two is stronger? It is not established that a mandatory injunction denotes that which is not mandatory; and yet, such is the case for those things connected by an equal application.
The expression of the definition applies to the view that the name itself is the denotation, as in the case of "the staff-bearers are going. Therefore, this position is superior.

Those [passages] possessing prior [correspondence] serve the purpose of restatement (*anuvāda*). It has been stated that the authority [of the Veda] is established through injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and the injunctive portions of mantras.

However, in this case, there is no status as a mantra regarding the "cake on eight potsherds" (*aṣṭākapāla*). Therefore, because it functions as a *codaka* (extended application), even the status of a name (*nāmadheya*) is not possible for the "cake on eight potsherds" and so forth, due to the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
However, whether it is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) or an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) is what is being doubted.
249] In that regard, it is not even doubted that it is an injunction of a subordinate quality, because there is no subject for such an injunction. How is there an absence of a subject?

Because of the cessation and production of different qualities; however, in the case of the *puroḍāśa* pan, it is not a subject of [the injunction] precisely because its purpose is non-existence (*abhāva*).

Likewise, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding the number twelve is not a praise by virtue of being connected to that [number], due to the cessation of other numbers, just as in the case of "The waters are peaceful. Therefore, since it is merely a mental impression (*pratibhā*), once again—
[Page 250] This is the objection regarding dependence.
Such being the case, some consider that validity is established through the prescription of a quality; what is their intention?

Does he not perceive production and cessation? No, he does not; because of the confusion arising from the syntactical unity (*sahavākya*), he considers it to be a single offering (*nirvāpa*) endowed with all the enumerations. Because of the unity of the sentence, the intention is that there is either a repetition of the ritual action or an option (*vikalpa*) among the qualities. [This applies to the statement] "The Vaiśvānara [cake] on twelve potsherds."
One considers the commencement to be for the sake of the deity.
To this it is replied: validity cannot be established through the prescription of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhāna*).

It cannot be stated because there is no subject matter [for such an injunction]. Now, it might be argued that the ritual dedicated to the deity Vaiśvānara is the subject matter. That is not so, because it would contradict the rule regarding the twelve potsherds (*dvādaśakapāla*). As for what was said—that the prescription of numbers is made by the passage beginning with "that which is on eight potsherds" (*yadaṣṭākapāla*)—that is poorly stated. How so?

Because the word *vaiśvānara* expresses a case-ending with a distinct referent, its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *dvādaśakapāla* is scripturally established. As for the phrases beginning with "that which is on eight potsherds," they purify one's spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).

The fact that Vaiśvānara is the locus of the ritual action is not understood from the syntactical connection of the words; rather, such a connection must be inferred on the grounds that the praise would otherwise be inexplicable. And it has already been stated that an inference is not tenable when the thing to be inferred is already established by other means.
If that is so, then it is merely a flash of intuition; no, for it is logically established as being for the purpose of praise (*stuti*). But how is its purpose as praise established?

It has been stated that because number has already been excluded by another number, [the reference to number] is for the sake of praise. For the exclusion occurs through verbal expression (*abhidhāna*), not through non-existence. Furthermore, a relationship is based on existence, not on verbal expression; for when existence is present, [the relationship] does not depend on verbal expression.
The designation by means of its constituent parts is thus justified.
254] But would it not follow that there is no comprehension of the relationship for that which has not been combined, precisely for the sake of its designation?

While separation can be effected, connection cannot likewise be separated. For the expression follows the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), not the actual state of things. Therefore, the praise is appropriate, just as in the case of "the waters are peaceful. And so it has been shown: "The rim and hub of this wheel are beautiful."

[Page 255] Even the prescription of a connection between qualities and results is not possible on this basis alone. Why? Because it is understood from this very source that they form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) for the purpose of praise (*stuti*). This has been demonstrated through the opening and the conclusion (*upakrama-upasaṃhāra*). Therefore—
Since its validity is established by way of being for the purpose of praise (*stuti*), its independence is proven;

that is its establishment. It has been stated that praise is possible through a connection based on partial designation (*avayutyābhidhāna*). However, where even the state of being related is not understood, and where the injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhāna*) is not possible—
As in the cases "The sacrificer is the cake-offering" (*yajamāna ekapālaḥ*) and "The sacrificer is the *prastara* grass-bundle," how is there validity in those instances?
But surely it was established in the section concerning the figurative and the primary (*gauṇamukhyādhikaraṇa*) that a figurative connection is a different matter—
[The opponent argues: "It occurs even for those [words] that denote [a primary object]. This very point is not tolerated. Why?
Because figurative application (*gauṇatā*) is simply not possible through a connection with another meaning. But how is it not possible?
For when there is figurative denotation, it is logical that only the qualities (*guṇa*) themselves should be the denoted objects; otherwise, the word "lion" would merely signify bravery in Devadatta.
It does not follow that the word "fire" conveys the tawny color in the boy;
for the word "lion," by way of the lion-genus, conveys qualities as many as there are connections with that genus.
One should convey those qualities as well, because there is no distinction [between them].
Now, if you think that when only that much is intended to be expressed, only that very thing is perceived—then word follows the speaker's intention, not the denoted object. What follows from that?

The secondary (gauṇa) [usage] consists in the superimposition of that nature [onto another]. And in the case of superimposition, there is no connection with a different object. Why? Because superimposition has as its domain only an object already apprehended; it does not touch an object not yet apprehended. It is grasped as "that very thing," not as "something similar to that."

Therefore, the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) is not capable of serving as a praise for either the grass-bundle (*prastara*) or the single potsherd (*ekakapāla*). Well then, let it be an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). But even that is impossible; for a quality being enjoined here must serve a functional purpose.
It is enjoined; and that [enjoining] is not tenable in either case. This has been demonstrated by the author of the Bhāṣya.
Therefore, this very doubt regarding *pratibhā* remains.
To this, it is replied: True, an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) is not possible, but an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is not [impossible].
It can be prevented. But has it not been said that it is not an *arthavāda* because it lacks a connection with the meaning?
What has been said is incorrect. How so? A figurative expression is possible precisely through its connection with its own primary meaning.

But was it not said that [the injunction] does not apply because there is no cognition of any quality connected with its own meaning? And was it not also said that the distinction arises from the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*)? True, this was said; however, it was also stated that when there is speaker’s intention, there is no connection with the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*). Consequently, praise (*stuti*) would be untenable. For what is connected with what?

To this it is replied: No, for you are indeed ignorant of the lack of restriction. When there is no intention to express the primary meaning, the utterance of the word "lion" is without a fixed basis; nor is it the case that there is no expression through superimposition by means of another word.

[The opponent] says: "Do not speak thus, O dull-witted one! For it is as the object of superimposition (*adhyāropa*) that the meaning 'lion' is intended to be expressed, not by way of a connection with its qualities. And this [superimposition] is not possible without the word 'lion';
therefore, the utterance of the word 'lion' is not without a basis. [The author] replies: "But was this not already stated by us?"

[261] Why is the meaning of "lion" superimposed upon Devadatta? If it is argued that this is because one perceives his qualities [to be like those of a lion], then it follows that the word must be presented as being connected to its primary referent. How, then, [is there a distinction]?

If it is argued that this is a figurative usage (*gauṇa*), we reply: no, because it is based on the observation of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) and because figurative usage is preceded by that primary sense (*mukhya*).
For even a primary object is established in its specific application through the observation of another means of valid cognition; how much more so, then, the figurative one?
What is the reasoning for "no"? How then is there such a thing as a "sky-flower"? It is exactly like the sky-flower itself.

Therefore, the status of an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) is established. The purpose and the manner [of its application] have been shown in the Bhāṣya. This applies equally to universals (*jāti*) and so forth. However, the individual topics (*adhikaraṇa*) are distinct because the refutations differ.

[Page 263] These are for the purpose of illustration. Therefore, the authority of those passages with figurative meanings is established by virtue of being *arthavādas* (explanatory praises), as is the case with those having metaphorical (*lākṣaṇika*) meanings. But how can there be metaphorical usage even in the accounts of creation and so forth?

What is the state of being the object of definition (*lakṣyatva*)? It is due to its connection with the same action as the objects of definition (*lakṣya*). Therefore, because it serves as the cause for being a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatva*), there is no contradiction in its being both the object of definition and the defining characteristic. How, then, is the word "animal" (*paśu*) applied to horses and the like?
By way of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), because the application [of the word] is preceded by a negation.

For a generic term (*jātiśabda*), when its application is negated among members of that same class, obtains its application only in a figurative sense (*gauṇatayā*) toward other members of that class. Why? Because a generic term, being negated with respect to one member of that class...

A quality that is inherent [in a thing] becomes the object of negation precisely by virtue of being what is to be negated. And because of the negation of that quality, when [the word] is applied to things belonging to that same class, it is understood as having a figurative (gauṇa) meaning. Therefore, there is no contradiction in saying that a genus-word (jātiśabda) is figurative. Consequently, its independence is established.
"In cases of doubt, [the meaning is determined] from the remainder of the sentence.

Now, one might object: has not the removal of doubt already been accomplished in the case of *yava*, *varāha*, and so forth, by means of the remainder of the sentence? True; however, that [removal of doubt] pertained to the meaning of the individual words (*padārtha*), whereas this [present case] concerns whether [a term] is innate (*autpattika*) or non-innate.
The object of doubt has been resolved: does a word have a meaning? Certainly it does.
268] How then is the innate relationship (*autpattikatva*) between the sentence and the sentence-meaning established through the usage of elders? True, that...
It was stated in the passage beginning with "tadbhūtānām" that [words] function as parts [of a whole]. Therefore, there is doubt regarding that which has already come into being (tadbhūte).

Here, however, the purpose is action (kriyārtha). This is the distinction between the meaning of individual words (padārtha) and the meaning of a sentence (vākyārtha), and this has been demonstrated in detail. Consequently, because of the doubt regarding the purpose of action, [the Veda] lacks authority. Such being the case, someone—

One might think that a determination regarding the conclusion is appropriate by virtue of the initial approach, because there is no contradiction; for a universal resides both in itself and in its particulars, just as in the case of the purpose of creation.
